title: [10.10] Implement same-sequence divergent-checkpoint fork detection and incident pathway.
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.10, item 8. Cross-refs: 9E.3 (Checkpointed policy frontier with rollback/fork protection - "Equal-sequence divergent content is treated as a fork incident requiring safe-mode entry and operator-visible forensics"), Top-10 links #3, #5, #10.

## What
Implement detection and incident handling for same-sequence divergent checkpoints (forks). When two checkpoints share the same `checkpoint_seq` but have different content (different `checkpoint_id`), this indicates either a compromised signer, a split-brain condition, or an implementation bug. The system must detect this condition, enter safe mode, and produce operator-visible forensic evidence.

## Detailed Requirements
- Fork detection: when accepting a checkpoint, check not only `seq > frontier.seq` but also verify that no previously-seen checkpoint with the same `seq` has a different `checkpoint_id`
- Maintain a persistent index of `(checkpoint_seq -> checkpoint_id)` for at least a configurable history window (default: 1000 checkpoints)
- On fork detection: immediately enter safe-mode (restricted operation mode where policy-gated actions are denied by default)
- Safe-mode behavior: reject all capability grants, deny extension activations, continue basic operation logging, emit continuous alerts
- Forensic evidence emission: produce a `ForkIncidentReport` containing both divergent checkpoints (full serialized objects), their signatures, the detection timestamp, and the local frontier state at detection time
- The fork incident report must be signed by the local node's key and persisted in the audit chain (bd-1lp)
- Operator notification: emit high-severity structured log events and, if configured, external alerting (webhook/signal)
- Recovery: safe-mode can only be exited by operator intervention (explicit acknowledgment of the fork incident and acceptance of a resolution checkpoint)
- No automatic resolution: the system must not attempt to pick a "winner" between forked checkpoints; this requires human judgment
- Fork detection must work even if the node has already accepted one of the forked checkpoints (retroactive detection via gossip/replication)

## Rationale
From plan section 9E.3: "Equal-sequence divergent content is treated as a fork incident requiring safe-mode entry and operator-visible forensics." A fork in the checkpoint chain is a critical security event. It means either (a) a signer's key was compromised and used to create a parallel chain, (b) the checkpoint creation system has a bug producing non-deterministic output, or (c) there is an active split-brain attack. In all cases, continuing normal operation risks policy confusion or authority bypass. Safe-mode entry is the conservative response that preserves security while awaiting operator resolution.

## Testing Requirements
- Unit tests: create two checkpoints with same seq but different content, verify fork detection triggers
- Unit tests: verify safe-mode entry on fork detection (policy-gated operations denied)
- Unit tests: verify ForkIncidentReport contains both divergent checkpoints with full detail
- Unit tests: verify forensic report is signed and persisted to audit chain
- Unit tests: verify safe-mode cannot be exited without explicit operator intervention
- Unit tests: verify retroactive fork detection (accept one checkpoint, then receive the divergent one)
- Integration tests: simulate split-brain scenario across two nodes, verify both detect the fork
- Integration tests: test safe-mode recovery workflow (operator acknowledges fork, provides resolution checkpoint)
- Adversarial tests: attempt normal operations during safe-mode, verify all are denied

## Implementation Notes
- The checkpoint history index can be a simple persistent map; it does not need to be large since forks should be extremely rare
- Safe-mode should be implemented as a global runtime state flag checked by all policy enforcement points
- Consider making safe-mode sticky across restarts (persisted state) so that a restart cannot be used to escape safe-mode
- The ForkIncidentReport should be designed for external consumption (operators, security teams, auditors)
- This is a low-frequency but high-severity code path; prioritize correctness and clarity over performance

## Dependencies
- Depends on: bd-1c7 (PolicyCheckpoint object for checkpoint structure), bd-lpl (checkpoint frontier for accepted checkpoint tracking)
- Blocks: bd-26o (conformance suite tests fork detection), bd-1lp (audit chain receives fork incident reports)

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Implement the full objective with explicit deterministic behavior, failure semantics, and rollback constraints where applicable.
2. Add focused unit tests covering normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid or adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
3. Add end-to-end or integration test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions and failure recovery paths using deterministic seeds or fixtures and CI-ready command lines.
4. Emit structured logs with stable fields (trace_id, decision_id, policy_id, component, event, outcome, error_code) and add assertions for critical log events in tests.
5. Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, replay/evidence pointers, benchmark/check outputs) and document operator verification steps.
6. For Rust build or test workflows introduced by this bead, document or execute via rch-wrapped commands for heavy compilation or test workloads.

title: [10.2] Define typed execution-slot registry and ABI contract for slot replacement
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.2, item 7. Cross-refs: 8.8 (Verified Self-Replacement Architecture), 9I.6, 10.15.

## What
Define the canonical execution-slot registry — the data structure and ABI contract that enables the Verified Self-Replacement Architecture. Each runtime component (parser, lowering passes, execution helpers, module primitives) is a typed 'slot' with explicit semantics contract, authority envelope, and promotion status. This is the foundation that allows delegate cells and native cells to be swapped transparently.

## Detailed Requirements
- Define SlotId type: unique identifier per replaceable runtime component
- Define SlotSemantics trait: the behavioral contract a cell must satisfy for a given slot
- Define AuthorityEnvelope: the maximum capability/effect set a cell in this slot may exercise
- Define PromotionStatus enum: {Delegate, NativeCandidate, NativePromoted, Demoted}
- Define SlotRegistry struct: registry of all slots with their current occupants, promotion history, and replacement lineage
- ABI contract: how cells are loaded, invoked, and replaced at runtime without breaking in-flight operations
- Deterministic serialization of registry state for replay and audit purposes
- Registry must be thread-safe (interior mutability with appropriate synchronization)
- No unsafe code (#![forbid(unsafe_code)] constraint)

## Rationale
The plan's Verified Self-Replacement Architecture (Section 8.8) is what enables FrankenEngine to ship security value early while the native VM matures. Without a formal slot registry and ABI contract, there's no way to systematically track, swap, and verify runtime components. This bead creates the mechanical foundation for the entire self-replacement program.

## Testing Requirements
- Unit tests: slot creation, registration, lookup, status transitions
- Unit tests: ABI contract enforcement — verify cells satisfy slot semantics
- Unit tests: authority envelope checks — verify cells cannot exceed declared authority
- Unit tests: deterministic serialization round-trips for registry state
- Unit tests: concurrent access patterns (multiple readers, exclusive writers)
- Integration test: register delegate cell → replace with native cell → verify promotion status → verify receipt
- Adversarial test: attempt to register cell that exceeds authority envelope → verify rejection
- E2E test: full replacement flow from delegate → native with signed receipt
- Structured logging: slot_id, cell_type, promotion_event, authority_check_pass, receipt_hash

title: [10.15] Add slot-level promotion gate runner (equivalence, capability-preservation, performance threshold, adversarial survival) with deterministic pass/fail artifact bundles.
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.15 (Delta Moonshots Execution Track), subsection 9I.6 (Verified Self-Replacement Architecture), item 3 of 8.

## What
Add a slot-level promotion gate runner that evaluates equivalence, capability-preservation, performance threshold, and adversarial survival criteria with deterministic pass/fail artifact bundles.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Promotion gauntlet gates (all must pass):
   - **Equivalence**: differential testing between delegate cell and native candidate across test262 normative profile + lockstep corpus. Zero semantic divergence required (failures produce minimized repro artifacts).
   - **Capability-preservation**: native candidate requests no capabilities beyond the slot's authority_envelope. Formal check against capability lattice.
   - **Performance threshold**: native candidate meets or exceeds configurable performance targets (latency, throughput) relative to delegate cell. No performance regression beyond tolerance.
   - **Adversarial survival**: native candidate passes the adversarial security corpus for its slot's attack surface. No new vulnerabilities introduced.
2. Gate runner execution:
   - Deterministic execution with pinned seeds and fixtures.
   - Per-gate pass/fail with structured evidence artifact (test results, benchmarks, security scan outputs).
   - Aggregate verdict with overall pass/fail and per-gate detail.
3. Output artifact bundle:
   - promotion_decision artifact (from bd-7rwi schema) with all gate results.
   - Per-gate evidence artifacts stored in evidence ledger.
   - Rollback token verified (rollback to delegate is tested as part of the gate).
4. Configurable gate strictness per slot (high-risk slots may require additional gates or stricter thresholds).
5. Gate results feed the replacement-lineage log and operator dashboard.

## Rationale
From 9I.6: "For each candidate native replacement, run promotion gauntlet: differential equivalence (test262 + lockstep corpus), capability-preservation proof, performance-threshold check, and adversarial survival suite." The promotion gate is the trust mechanism that ensures native replacements are genuinely equivalent or better than delegates, not just untested substitutions.

## Testing Requirements
- Unit tests: each gate evaluation with known-pass and known-fail inputs, aggregate verdict logic.
- Integration tests: full gate run for a representative slot replacement (delegate -> native candidate).
- Regression tests: known-bad native candidates must fail the appropriate gate.
- Meta-tests: verify rollback-token testing works (rollback to delegate actually succeeds).

## Implementation Notes
- Reuse test262 and lockstep infrastructure from 10.7.
- Performance benchmarks should use the infrastructure from 10.6.
- Adversarial tests should draw from the security corpus in 10.7.

## Dependencies
- bd-7rwi (self-replacement schema for promotion_decision artifact).
- bd-3ciq (delegate cell harness provides the comparison baseline).
- 10.7 (test262, lockstep, and adversarial test infrastructure).
- 10.6 (performance benchmark infrastructure).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Implement the full objective with deterministic behavior, explicit failure semantics, and safe fallback/rollback rules.
- Add focused unit tests for normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid or adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
- Add integration and/or end-to-end test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions, degraded mode, and recovery behavior with deterministic fixtures.
- Emit structured logs with stable keys (trace_id, decision_id, policy_id, component, event, outcome, error_code) and assert critical events in tests.
- Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, evidence pointers, replay pointers, benchmark/check outputs) plus clear operator verification steps.
- Ensure heavy Rust build/test execution paths are documented and run through rch wrappers when implementation begins.

title: [10.15] Add deterministic fallback policy: when attestation validation fails or expires, high-impact autonomous actions degrade to conservative safe mode.
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.15 (Delta Moonshots Execution Track), subsection 9I.1 (TEE-Bound Cryptographic Decision Receipts), item 4 of 4.

## What
Implement a deterministic fallback policy that degrades high-impact autonomous actions to conservative safe mode when TEE attestation validation fails or attestation evidence expires, ensuring the system never silently operates without hardware-rooted trust.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Define action classification tiers (high-impact, standard, low-impact) that determine attestation requirements:
   - High-impact: quarantine, terminate, emergency grant, policy promotion, capability escalation -- require valid attestation or degrade.
   - Standard: routine monitoring, evidence collection -- warn on attestation failure but continue.
   - Low-impact: logging, metrics -- no attestation requirement.
2. Fallback behavior for high-impact actions when attestation is unavailable:
   - Switch to challenge/sandbox-first mode (no autonomous execution of high-impact actions).
   - Queue pending decisions with explicit "attestation-pending" status.
   - Emit structured alert to operator surfaces with degradation reason and estimated restoration path.
   - Continue emitting software-signed receipts with explicit `attestation_status: degraded` field.
3. Automatic restoration: when attestation becomes available again, validate backlog and resume normal operation with audit trail of degraded period.
4. Hard timeout: if attestation remains unavailable beyond configurable threshold, escalate to operator-mandatory review.
5. Fallback activation/deactivation must be atomic and produce signed transition receipts.
6. No silent fallback: every transition to/from degraded mode must be logged, alerted, and receipt-linked.

## Rationale
From 9I.1: "Fallback semantics are explicit: if attestation freshness/proof fails, high-impact autonomous actions degrade to deterministic safe mode (challenge/sandbox-first) until trust is restored." This ensures the system fails safe rather than silently losing its strongest trust guarantee. The risk register also notes the importance of deterministic fallback modes for operational complexity management.

## Testing Requirements
- Unit tests: verify each action tier correctly triggers/bypasses fallback, test boundary conditions on freshness expiry, test atomic transition semantics.
- Integration tests: simulate attestation provider failure mid-operation, verify queued decisions are handled correctly on restoration, verify operator alerts fire.
- Chaos tests: random attestation failures during decision pipeline execution to verify no decisions leak through without proper degradation handling.
- Deterministic replay: degraded-mode decisions must be fully replayable with identical fallback behavior given identical attestation-state inputs.

## Implementation Notes
- Use a state machine pattern for attestation status (Valid -> Degraded -> Restored -> Valid) with explicit transition guards.
- Degradation state should be observable via frankentui operator surfaces and metrics endpoints.
- Consider integration with the sentinel evidence stream so attestation degradation events feed risk scoring.

## Dependencies
- bd-2xu5 (TEE attestation policy for freshness windows and validation rules).
- bd-3ab3 (verifier pipeline that detects attestation failures).
- 10.5 (extension host decision contract infrastructure for action classification).
- 10.8 (operational readiness for safe-mode startup semantics).

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Implement the full objective with explicit deterministic behavior, failure semantics, and rollback constraints where applicable.
2. Add focused unit tests covering normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid or adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
3. Add end-to-end or integration test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions and failure recovery paths using deterministic seeds or fixtures and CI-ready command lines.
4. Emit structured logs with stable fields (trace_id, decision_id, policy_id, component, event, outcome, error_code) and add assertions for critical log events in tests.
5. Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, replay/evidence pointers, benchmark/check outputs) and document operator verification steps.
6. For Rust build or test workflows introduced by this bead, document or execute via rch-wrapped commands for heavy compilation or test workloads.

title: [PARSER-PHASE-4] Mathematical Error Recovery (Bayesian Diagnostics)
description:
## Change:
Implement Bayesian syntax-error recovery controller with strict bounded attempts, explicit confidence calibration, and execution-safe fallback semantics.

## Hotspot evidence:
Hardcoded parser recovery heuristics can mis-repair syntax and create misleading downstream semantics; current strategy needs principled decisioning with deterministic guardrails.

## Mapped graveyard sections:

- `high_level_summary_of_frankensuite_planned_and_implemented_features_and_concepts.md` §0.16, §0.19, §1994

## EV score:
(Impact 4 * Confidence 3 * Reuse 4) / (Effort 4 * Friction 3) = 4.0

## Priority tier:
A

## Adoption wedge:
Use as tooling/diagnostic mode first; execution mode defaults to strict parse-fail unless confidence and policy criteria are met.

## Budgeted mode:
- Max recovery attempts per file
- Max token-skips per attempt
- Max inserted-token edits
- On exhaustion: deterministic parse failure (no speculative continuation)

## Expected-loss model:
States:
- `S_recoverable`: file has local syntax defect recoverable without semantic distortion
- `S_ambiguous`: multiple plausible repairs
- `S_unrecoverable`: reliable repair not possible
Actions:
- `A_recover_continue`, `A_partial_recover`, `A_fail_strict`
Loss matrix:
- `L(A_recover_continue,S_unrecoverable)=90`
- `L(A_recover_continue,S_ambiguous)=55`
- `L(A_fail_strict,S_recoverable)=12`
- `L(A_partial_recover,S_ambiguous)=15`

## Calibration + fallback trigger:
- Fail strict if posterior confidence < threshold.
- Fail strict if recovery path violates deterministic progression invariant.
- Fail strict if recovered AST fails oracle parity checks.

## Isomorphism proof plan:
- Evaluate recovered outputs against curated repaired-golden corpus.
- For execution-admissible recoveries, require semantic equivalence checks on declared invariant set.
- Record decision ledger tuple `(evidence, posterior, action, loss)` per recovery.

## p50/p95/p99 before/after target:
- Recovery-mode false-positive repair rate <= 2%
- Recovery-mode success on common typo corpus >= 90%
- Strict mode parse latency non-regression within +10% p99

## Primary failure risk + countermeasure:
Risk: overconfident repair induces silent semantic corruption.
Countermeasure: conservative loss matrix, strict confidence threshold, and execution-mode default-to-fail policy.

## Repro artifact pack:
- `artifacts/parser_phase4_recovery/baseline.json`
- `artifacts/parser_phase4_recovery/recovery_decision_log.jsonl`

## Primary paper status (checklist):
Status: hypothesis
- [ ] Bayesian recovery references reviewed
- [ ] calibration methodology documented
- [ ] false-positive tradeoff analysis captured
- [ ] promotion policy approved

## Interference test status:
Requires interference report from parallel path gate (`bd-3rjg`) before enabling recovery atop parallel parser mode.

## Demo linkage:
- `demo_id`: `demo.parser.phase4.bayesian_recovery`
- `claim_id`: `claim.parser.phase4.safe_error_recovery`

## Rollback:
Disable recovery controller and run strict parse-fail mode only if calibration, parity, or deterministic-progression checks fail.

## Baseline comparator:
Ad-hoc heuristic recovery and strict parse-fail behavior currently in use.

## Detailed sub-tasks:
1. Define evidence features and posterior update math.
2. Define conservative loss matrix and policy thresholds.
3. Implement deterministic bounded-recovery engine.
4. Add decision/evidence logging and replay checks.
5. Validate against repaired-golden corpus and oracle gate.

## User-outcome optimization addendum:
- Recovery behavior must be transparent: users need to know when the parser repaired input, what changed, and why strict failure was chosen otherwise.
- Keep strict mode as default safety path while exposing diagnostic recovery reports for editor and tooling workflows.
- Recovery explanations should include confidence, selected action, rejected alternatives, and deterministic replay token.

## Mandatory test and e2e contract:
- Unit tests: posterior update math, loss matrix decision policy, bounded-attempt invariants, deterministic action selection, explanation generator.
- Integration tests: strict-vs-recovery mode behavior, oracle parity post-recovery, composition with serial and parallel parser modes, fallback trigger correctness.

- Emit deterministic repair-diff artifact (`repair_diff.jsonl`) so users can inspect exactly what the recovery controller changed.
- Add explicit mode policy table: `strict_default`, `diagnostic_recovery`, `execution_recovery` with hard safety boundaries.

title: [AUDIT] hostcall_telemetry: record constructor seeds placeholder hash

Suggested fix: Build the canonical hash from an immutable pre-record tuple before constructing HostcallTelemetryRecord, or use a dedicated constructor that never materializes a placeholder content_hash in production state.

title: [10.15] Add frankensqlite-backed provenance index supporting deterministic source-to-sink lineage queries and replay joins.
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.15 (Delta Moonshots Execution Track), subsection 9I.7 (Runtime IFC), cross-cutting storage item.

## What
Add a frankensqlite-backed provenance index supporting deterministic source-to-sink lineage queries and replay joins for IFC evidence.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Storage schema:
   - **Flow events table**: stores flow-check events (allowed, blocked, declassified) with: event_id, extension_id, source_label, sink_clearance, flow_location (code path ref), decision (allowed/blocked/declassified), receipt_ref, timestamp.
   - **Flow proofs table**: stores flow_proof artifacts indexed by proof_id, extension_id, source_label, sink_clearance, proof_method, epoch_id.
   - **Declassification receipts table**: stores declassification_receipt artifacts indexed by receipt_id, extension_id, decision, source_label, sink_clearance, timestamp.
   - **Confinement claims table**: stores confinement_claim artifacts indexed by claim_id, extension_id, claim_strength, epoch_id.
   - **Provenance chain index**: source-to-sink lineage queries -- given a data source label, trace all possible flows through the system to sinks with evidence of each hop.
2. Deterministic queries:
   - Source-to-sink lineage: given source_label, return all proven flow paths to sinks with proof references.
   - Sink provenance: given sink, return all data sources that have flowed to it with evidence chain.
   - Extension confinement status: aggregate flow proof coverage for an extension.

title: [10.5] Port extension lifecycle manager into compile-active modules.
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.5, item 2 (Port extension lifecycle manager into compile-active modules). Cross-refs: 9A.8 (resource budgets per extension), 9G.2 (cancellation as protocol, not afterthought), 9A.1 (capability-typed execution model).

## What
Implement a deterministic extension lifecycle state machine that governs every extension from load through termination. The lifecycle states are: `Unloaded -> Validating -> Loading -> Starting -> Running -> Suspending -> Suspended -> Resuming -> Terminating -> Terminated -> Quarantined`. Each transition is guarded by explicit preconditions (validated manifest, resource budget allocated, capability set confirmed). The lifecycle manager is a compile-active module, meaning its state machine transitions and guard predicates are expressed in the type system where possible, preventing invalid transitions at compile time.

## Detailed Requirements
- Define `ExtensionState` enum with all lifecycle states listed above.
- Define `LifecycleTransition` enum representing valid transitions (e.g., `Start`, `Suspend`, `Resume`, `Terminate`, `Quarantine`).
- Implement `ExtensionLifecycleManager` struct that holds current state, validated manifest reference, resource budget handle, and a transition log.
- Each transition method must: (a) verify precondition (current state allows transition), (b) execute transition logic, (c) emit structured lifecycle event to telemetry, (d) update state atomically.
- Invalid transitions must return `LifecycleError` with deterministic error messages including `extension_id`, `current_state`, `attempted_transition`.
- Implement cancellation protocol per 9G.2: `Terminate` must be a cooperative protocol with a timeout fallback to forced termination. The extension gets a `cancel_token` and has a configurable grace period (default 5s, max 30s) before forced kill.
- Resource budget enforcement per 9A.8: each lifecycle transition checks remaining budget (CPU time, memory, hostcall count). Budget exhaustion triggers automatic `Suspend` or `Terminate` depending on policy.
- The lifecycle manager must be `Send + Sync` for use across async task boundaries.
- All state transitions must be logged with monotonic timestamps for replay.

## Rationale
Extensions are untrusted code running inside the engine. Without a rigorous lifecycle manager, extensions could enter inconsistent states, leak resources, or evade termination. The compile-active approach ensures that the type system prevents coding errors in lifecycle management itself. The cancellation protocol (9G.2) ensures that termination is never silent or abrupt without giving the extension a chance to clean up, while the timeout fallback ensures the runtime cannot be held hostage.

## Testing Requirements
- **Unit tests**: Test every valid state transition. Test every invalid transition is rejected with correct error. Test cancellation with cooperative shutdown. Test cancellation with timeout-forced shutdown. Test budget exhaustion triggers correct containment.
- **State machine exhaustiveness**: Property test that from every reachable state, only documented transitions are possible.
- **Integration tests**: Full lifecycle of a mock extension: load -> validate -> start -> run -> suspend -> resume -> terminate. Verify telemetry events emitted at each transition.
- **Concurrency tests**: Multiple extensions running concurrently with independent lifecycle managers, verifying no cross-contamination.
- **Determinism tests**: Replay a recorded transition sequence and verify identical state sequence and telemetry output.

## Implementation Notes
- Consider using a typestate pattern in Rust (`ExtensionLifecycle<Running>`, `ExtensionLifecycle<Suspended>`) for compile-time transition safety, with a dynamic fallback for runtime-driven transitions.
- The transition log should be an append-only `Vec<LifecycleEvent>` with each event containing `(monotonic_timestamp, from_state, to_state, trigger, decision_id)`.
- Integrate with the telemetry recorder (bd-5pk) for structured event emission.
- Resource budget handles should be opaque tokens obtained from the resource subsystem (10.4 module surface).

## Dependencies
- **Blocked by**: bd-xq7 (manifest validation - lifecycle manager requires a validated manifest to proceed past `Validating` state).
- **Blocks**: bd-5pk (telemetry needs lifecycle events), bd-2gl (containment actions are lifecycle transitions), bd-375 (delegate cells use the same lifecycle manager).
- **Parent**: bd-1yq (10.5 epic).

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Implement the full objective with explicit deterministic behavior, failure semantics, and rollback constraints where applicable.
2. Add focused unit tests covering normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid/adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
3. Add end-to-end/integration test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions and failure recovery paths using deterministic seeds/fixtures and CI-ready command lines.
4. Emit structured logs with stable fields (`trace_id`, `decision_id`, `policy_id`, `component`, `event`, `outcome`, `error_code`) and add assertions for critical log events in tests.
5. Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, replay/evidence pointers, benchmark/check outputs) and document operator verification steps.
6. For Rust build/test workflows introduced by this bead, document/execute via `rch`-wrapped commands for heavy compilation/test workloads.

title: [10.5] Implement runtime flow-label propagation at dynamic hostcall boundaries and enforce sink-clearance checks.
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.5, item 9 (Implement runtime flow-label propagation at dynamic hostcall boundaries). Cross-refs: 9I.7 (IFC + Deterministic Exfiltration Prevention), 10.2 (IFC flow-lattice in VM core), 9A.7 (capability lattice integrates with flow labels).

## What
Implement Information Flow Control (IFC) enforcement at runtime hostcall boundaries for dynamic paths that could not be verified statically. Every value crossing a hostcall boundary carries a flow label indicating its secrecy and integrity classification. The runtime propagation layer checks that the flow label of data being sent to a sink (e.g., network egress, file write, IPC channel) is compatible with the sink's clearance level. If the flow label exceeds the sink's clearance, the hostcall is blocked and the violation is recorded as evidence for the Guardplane. This is the runtime complement to the static IFC analysis in 10.2.

## Detailed Requirements
- Define `FlowLabel` struct: `{ secrecy: SecrecyLevel, integrity: IntegrityLevel }` where `SecrecyLevel` and `IntegrityLevel` are elements of a configurable lattice (partial order).
- Define `SecrecyLevel` enum with at least: `Public`, `Internal`, `Confidential`, `Secret`, `TopSecret` (configurable/extensible).
- Define `IntegrityLevel` enum with at least: `Untrusted`, `Validated`, `Verified`, `Trusted` (configurable/extensible).
- Implement `FlowLabelLattice` that defines the partial order: `can_flow(from: &FlowLabel, to: &FlowLabel) -> bool` returns true iff `from.secrecy <= to.secrecy` AND `from.integrity >= to.integrity` (standard Bell-LaPadula + Biba).
- Implement `SinkClearance` struct: `{ max_secrecy: SecrecyLevel, min_integrity: IntegrityLevel }` defining what data a sink is authorized to receive.
- Implement runtime flow-label propagation at hostcall dispatch:
  - Every hostcall argument carries a `FlowLabel` (attached via a `Labeled<T>` wrapper or context parameter).
  - Before executing a sink-type hostcall (FsWrite, NetworkSend, IpcSend), the dispatcher checks `can_flow(argument_label, sink_clearance)`.
  - If the check fails: block the hostcall, return `HostcallResult::Denied { reason: FlowViolation }`, emit a `FlowViolationEvent` to telemetry, and provide the violation as evidence to the Guardplane.
  - If the check passes: execute the hostcall normally, propagate the label to the output.
- Label join semantics for operations that combine multiple labeled values: `join(a, b) = FlowLabel { secrecy: max(a.secrecy, b.secrecy), integrity: min(a.integrity, b.integrity) }`.
- Flow labels must be immutable once assigned (no downgrading without explicit declassification through bd-3jy).
- Labels must be propagated through IPC channels: when an extension sends data to another extension via IPC, the receiving extension inherits the label.
- Performance: flow-label checking must add < 500ns overhead per hostcall.

## Rationale
Static IFC analysis (10.2) can verify many flow constraints at compile time, but dynamic hostcall paths -- especially those involving runtime-computed capabilities, user-provided data, or IPC between extensions -- cannot be fully analyzed statically. Runtime flow-label propagation closes this gap by enforcing IFC invariants at every hostcall boundary. Per 9I.7, the engine must prevent deterministic exfiltration: a compromised extension must not be able to send secret data to an unauthorized sink. The runtime layer is the last line of defense before data actually leaves the extension boundary.

## Testing Requirements
- **Unit tests**: `can_flow` with all lattice level combinations (authorized and unauthorized). Label join produces correct result. `Labeled<T>` wrapper preserves the label through operations.
- **Hostcall dispatch tests**: A hostcall with a `Secret`-labeled argument to a `Public`-clearance network sink is blocked. A hostcall with a `Public`-labeled argument to a `Secret`-clearance sink is allowed. Verify telemetry records the violation/pass.
- **IPC propagation tests**: Extension A sends `Confidential` data to Extension B via IPC; Extension B's subsequent hostcalls carry the `Confidential` label. Extension B attempts to send that data to a `Public` sink; verify it is blocked.
- **Performance tests**: Benchmark flow-label checking overhead; assert < 500ns per hostcall.
- **Integration tests**: Full pipeline: extension makes hostcalls with various labels, some pass, some are blocked. Verify Guardplane receives flow violations as evidence and adjusts posterior accordingly.
- **Edge case tests**: Default label for unlabeled data (should be maximally restrictive: `TopSecret`/`Untrusted`). Label for system-generated data (should be `Public`/`Trusted`).

## Implementation Notes
- The `Labeled<T>` wrapper should be zero-cost when the label is statically known (use generics with const labels where possible).
- Flow-label checking is a simple comparison in the partial order; implement as integer comparison on the ordinal values for performance.
- The lattice configuration should be loadable from a policy file to support custom secrecy/integrity levels per deployment.
- Integration point: the telemetry recorder (bd-5pk) already has a `flow_label` field in `HostcallTelemetryRecord`; this bead populates that field.
- The IPC label propagation requires cooperation with the IPC subsystem (10.4 module surface); define a trait interface that the IPC layer implements.

## Dependencies
- **Blocked by**: bd-5pk (telemetry records flow violations), 10.2 (IFC flow-lattice defines the lattice structure; this bead uses it at runtime).
- **Blocks**: bd-3jy (declassification is the controlled way to change flow labels), bd-375 (delegate cells must have flow-label enforcement).
- **Parent**: bd-1yq (10.5 epic).

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Implement the full objective with explicit deterministic behavior, failure semantics, and rollback constraints where applicable.
2. Add focused unit tests covering normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid/adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
3. Add end-to-end/integration test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions and failure recovery paths using deterministic seeds/fixtures and CI-ready command lines.
4. Emit structured logs with stable fields (`trace_id`, `decision_id`, `policy_id`, `component`, `event`, `outcome`, `error_code`) and add assertions for critical log events in tests.
5. Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, replay/evidence pointers, benchmark/check outputs) and document operator verification steps.
6. For Rust build/test workflows introduced by this bead, document/execute via `rch`-wrapped commands for heavy compilation/test workloads.

title: [10.11] Define canonical runtime capability profiles (`FullCaps`, `EngineCoreCaps`, `PolicyCaps`, `RemoteCaps`, `ComputeOnlyCaps`) and enforce them at API boundaries.
description:
## Plan Reference
- **Section**: 10.11 item 1 (FrankenSQLite-Inspired Runtime Systems Track)
- **9G Cross-ref**: 9G.1 — Capability-context-first runtime (Cx threading)
- **Top-10 Links**: #2 (Probabilistic Guardplane), #7 (Capability lattice + typed policy DSL), #8 (Per-extension resource budget)

## What
Define canonical runtime capability profiles (`FullCaps`, `EngineCoreCaps`, `PolicyCaps`, `RemoteCaps`, `ComputeOnlyCaps`) as concrete Rust types and enforce them at every API boundary in the engine and extension-host crates. These profiles partition the full authority universe into narrow, composable subsets so that each subsystem receives only the capabilities it needs.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Define a `Capability` trait hierarchy and five canonical profile structs:
   - `FullCaps`: union of all capabilities; only available to top-level orchestrator and test harness.
   - `EngineCoreCaps`: VM dispatch, GC, IR lowering — no network, no policy mutation, no extension lifecycle.
   - `PolicyCaps`: policy read/write, evidence emission, decision-contract invocation — no direct VM dispatch, no raw network.
   - `RemoteCaps`: network egress, lease management, idempotency-key derivation — no policy mutation, no direct VM execution.
   - `ComputeOnlyCaps`: pure computation with zero side effects — no I/O, no network, no policy, no evidence emission.
2. Each profile must be a zero-cost compile-time marker where possible (generic bounds, sealed traits); runtime checks are fallback-only for dynamic dispatch paths.
3. API boundaries (public trait methods, hostcall entry points, scheduler task constructors) must declare their required capability profile as a generic bound or explicit parameter.
4. Attempting to invoke an operation without the required profile must fail at compile time where statically checkable, or return a typed `CapabilityDenied` error at runtime.
5. Profile composition rules: profiles may be intersected (narrowing) but never unioned outside `FullCaps`; widening requires explicit `escalation_receipt` evidence artifact.
6. Integration with `Cx`: capability profiles must be threaded through or embedded within the `Cx` context object so that control-plane and data-plane boundaries carry authority evidence.
7. Serialization: each profile must have a canonical deterministic serialization for inclusion in evidence-ledger entries and replay artifacts.

## Rationale
This is the foundational authority-control primitive for the entire runtime. Without typed capability profiles enforced at API boundaries, ambient authority leaks silently and the security doctrine (Section 6) cannot be upheld. By making authority a type-system property (9G.1), the engine structurally prevents privilege escalation and enables downstream proof-carrying specialization (Section 8.9) where tighter envelopes yield faster code paths.

## Testing Requirements
- **Unit tests**: Verify each profile grants exactly the expected capability set. Verify compile-time rejection of mismatched profiles (via `trybuild` or equivalent negative-compilation tests). Verify `CapabilityDenied` error on runtime dynamic-dispatch paths.
- **Property tests**: Fuzz profile intersection/composition to confirm monotonic narrowing and that no composition produces capabilities outside the declared union.
- **Integration tests**: End-to-end scenario where an extension-host task attempts operations requiring `RemoteCaps` while holding only `ComputeOnlyCaps`; verify denial, structured error, and evidence emission.
- **Logging/observability**: All capability checks must emit structured log events with fields: `trace_id`, `component`, `required_profile`, `held_profile`, `outcome` (granted/denied), `error_code`.
- **Reproducibility**: Profile definitions must be snapshot-stable across builds; canonical serialization must produce identical bytes for identical profiles.

## Implementation Notes
- Crate location: `crates/franken-engine` (profile definitions) + `crates/franken-extension-host` (enforcement at hostcall boundaries).
- Use Rust sealed-trait pattern to prevent external implementations of capability profiles.
- Consider `typestate` pattern for zero-cost compile-time enforcement on hot paths.
- Coordinate with `Cx` type from `franken-kernel` (10.13 integration); profiles should embed into `Cx` without coupling VM hot loops to control-plane internals (Section 8.4.4 anti-coupling constraint).
- Heavy compilation workloads should use `rch`-wrapped commands per project convention.

## Dependencies
- Depends on: `franken-kernel` `Cx` type definition (10.13 provides integration; this bead defines the primitive profiles).
- Blocks: bd-1za (compile-time audit gate), bd-hli (remote capability gating), bd-2ao (region-quiescence close), and all downstream beads that reference capability profiles.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Implement the full objective with explicit deterministic behavior, failure semantics, and rollback constraints where applicable.
2. Add focused unit tests covering normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid or adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
3. Add end-to-end or integration test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions and failure recovery paths using deterministic seeds or fixtures and CI-ready command lines.
4. Emit structured logs with stable fields (trace_id, decision_id, policy_id, component, event, outcome, error_code) and add assertions for critical log events in tests.
5. Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, replay/evidence pointers, benchmark/check outputs) and document operator verification steps.
6. For Rust build or test workflows introduced by this bead, document or execute via rch-wrapped commands for heavy compilation or test workloads.

title: [10.11] Implement saga orchestrator for multi-step publish/evict/quarantine workflows with deterministic compensation.
description:
## Plan Reference
- **Section**: 10.11 item 24 (FrankenSQLite-Inspired Runtime Systems Track)
- **9G Cross-ref**: 9G.7 — Remote-effects contract for distributed runtime operations
- **Top-10 Links**: #5 (Supply-chain trust fabric), #10 (Provenance + revocation fabric)

## What
Implement a saga orchestrator for multi-step publish/evict/quarantine workflows with deterministic compensation. Multi-step distributed operations (e.g., quarantine an extension across fleet nodes, publish a revocation and propagate it, evict cached artifacts and confirm cleanup) are modeled as sagas with explicit forward steps and compensating actions.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Define a \`Saga\` type:
   - \`saga_id\`: unique identifier derived from trace context.
   - \`steps\`: ordered list of \`SagaStep\` instances, each with:
     - \`step_name\`: maps to a named computation in the registry (bd-3s3).
     - \`forward_action\`: the primary operation to execute.
     - \`compensating_action\`: the rollback operation if a later step fails.
     - \`idempotency_key\`: derived per bd-359.
     - \`timeout\`: maximum duration for step completion.
     - \`lease_id\`: associated liveness lease (bd-18m).
   - \`state\`: \`Pending | InProgress(step_index) | Compensating(step_index) | Completed | Failed(diagnostic)\`.
2. Execution protocol:
   - Execute steps in order. After each successful step, persist the saga state to durable storage.
   - If a step fails, execute compensating actions in reverse order for all previously completed steps.
   - Each step uses idempotency keys for safe retry.
   - Each step is lease-backed: if the lease expires during step execution, the step is cancelled.
3. Deterministic compensation: compensating actions must be deterministic given the same inputs. Compensation state is persisted so that partially-compensated sagas can resume after crashes.
4. Saga types for required workflows:
   - \`QuarantineSaga\`: suspend extension -> flush evidence -> propagate quarantine -> confirm.
   - \`RevocationSaga\`: emit revocation -> propagate to peers -> confirm convergence -> update frontier.
   - \`EvictionSaga\`: mark for eviction -> drain active references -> delete artifacts -> confirm cleanup.
   - \`PublishSaga\`: validate artifact -> stage -> commit -> notify subscribers.
5. Evidence: every saga state transition emits a structured evidence entry: \`saga_id\`, \`saga_type\`, \`step_name\`, \`step_index\`, \`action\` (forward/compensate), \`result\`, \`trace_id\`, \`epoch_id\`.
6. The orchestrator runs as a supervised service (bd-2gg) with \`Permanent\` restart policy. On restart, it resumes any in-progress sagas from persisted state.

## Rationale
Multi-step distributed operations are the most complex failure surface in the runtime. Without structured saga orchestration, partial failures leave inconsistent state: a quarantine that propagated to some nodes but not others, a revocation that was emitted but not confirmed. The 9G.7 contract requires deterministic compensation so that the system can always reach a consistent state regardless of where failures occur. Saga persistence ensures crash recovery, and idempotency keys ensure retry safety.

## Testing Requirements
- **Unit tests**: Verify saga step execution in order. Verify compensation in reverse order on failure. Verify idempotency-key usage per step. Verify state persistence after each step. Verify crash recovery from persisted state.
- **Property tests**: Inject failures at random saga steps; verify compensation always runs for all completed steps and produces consistent final state.
- **Integration tests**: Execute a \`QuarantineSaga\` with a simulated node failure at step 2; verify compensation rolls back step 1, evidence is emitted for each transition, and the saga state is consistent after recovery.
- **Crash recovery test**: Execute a saga, crash mid-step (in lab runtime), restart, and verify saga resumes from persisted state.
- **Logging/observability**: Saga events carry full structured fields for forensic reconstruction.

## Implementation Notes
- Saga state persistence should use frankensqlite (10.14) with WAL mode for crash safety.
- Each saga step should be executed as a named computation via the remote computation registry (bd-3s3) with idempotency keys (bd-359) and lease backing (bd-18m).
- The orchestrator should support concurrent saga execution with configurable concurrency limits (bulkhead from bd-289).
- Consider a DSL or builder pattern for saga definition to reduce boilerplate.

## Dependencies
- Depends on: bd-3s3 (named computations for saga steps), bd-359 (idempotency keys for retry safety), bd-18m (lease-backed liveness for step timeout), bd-2gg (supervision tree for orchestrator lifecycle), bd-hli (remote capability gate).
- Blocks: 10.13 integration (quarantine/revocation workflows), 10.12 (fleet containment sagas).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Implement the full objective with deterministic behavior, explicit failure semantics, and safe fallback/rollback rules.
- Add focused unit tests for normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid or adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
- Add integration and/or end-to-end test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions, degraded mode, and recovery behavior with deterministic fixtures.
- Emit structured logs with stable keys (trace_id, decision_id, policy_id, component, event, outcome, error_code) and assert critical events in tests.
- Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, evidence pointers, replay pointers, benchmark/check outputs) plus clear operator verification steps.
- Ensure heavy Rust build/test execution paths are documented and run through rch wrappers when implementation begins.

6. For Rust build/test workflows introduced by this bead, document or execute via rch-wrapped commands for heavy compilation/test workloads.

# Enrichment: Concrete E2E Test Scenario, Logging Field Specs, Implementation Approach

## Concrete E2E Test Scenario: QuarantineSaga with Mid-Step Failure and Compensation

### Setup
1. Create a `SagaOrchestrator` backed by an in-memory durable store (simulating frankensqlite WAL).
2. Register 4 named computations in the registry: `suspend_extension`, `flush_evidence`, `propagate_quarantine`, `confirm_quarantine`.
3. Register 4 compensating computations: `resume_extension`, `noop` (evidence flush is idempotent), `retract_quarantine`, `noop`.
4. Create `RemoteInFlight` bulkhead with `max_concurrent: 2` and `SagaExecution` bulkhead with `max_concurrent: 1`.
5. Seed extension `ext-suspect-001` in `Active` state.
6. Configure `LeaseStore` with TTL = 5s for operation leases.
7. Set up a mock `RemoteNode` for quarantine propagation that will FAIL on first call (simulating network error).

### Exercise
1. **Create QuarantineSaga**: `saga = orchestrator.create(QuarantineSaga { target: "ext-suspect-001" })`. Verify: `saga.state == Pending`, saga persisted to durable store.
2. **Execute step 1 (suspend)**: `orchestrator.execute_next(saga_id)`. Verify: `ext-suspect-001.state == Suspended`, saga state persisted as `InProgress(1)`.
3. **Execute step 2 (flush evidence)**: `orchestrator.execute_next(saga_id)`. Verify: evidence flushed, saga state `InProgress(2)`.
4. **Execute step 3 (propagate) — FAILS**: `orchestrator.execute_next(saga_id)`. Mock remote node fails. Verify: saga transitions to `Compensating(2)`.
5. **Compensation step 2 (noop)**: Orchestrator runs compensation. Saga transitions to `Compensating(1)`.
6. **Compensation step 1 (resume extension)**: Orchestrator runs compensation. `ext-suspect-001.state == Active` (restored). Saga transitions to `Failed(diagnostic)`.
7. **Retry saga**: Reconfigure mock remote node to succeed. Create new saga for same target (new idempotency keys). Execute all 4 steps. Verify: saga transitions to `Completed`.

### Crash Recovery Scenario (steps 8-10)
8. **Create a new PublishSaga**: Start saga, execute steps 1 and 2 successfully. Saga state persisted as `InProgress(2)`.
9. **Simulate crash**: Drop the `SagaOrchestrator` mid-execution (between step 2 and step 3).
10. **Restart**: Create new `SagaOrchestrator` from persisted store. Verify: orchestrator detects in-progress saga, resumes from step 3 (not step 1).

### Assert
1. Steps 1-6: exactly 6 evidence entries emitted (one per step forward + compensation): `step_1_forward`, `step_2_forward`, `step_3_forward_failed`, `step_2_compensate`, `step_1_compensate`, `saga_failed`.
2. Step 4: saga state after failure == `Compensating(2)`, not `Failed` directly (compensation runs first).
3. Step 6: `ext-suspect-001` is back in `Active` state (compensation succeeded).
4. Step 7 (retry): new saga has different `saga_id` and different idempotency keys (no collision with failed saga).
5. Step 7: saga ends in `Completed` state with 4 forward evidence entries + 1 completion entry.
6. Step 10: restarted orchestrator resumes saga from persisted state, does NOT re-execute steps 1 and 2.
7. Bulkhead: during saga execution, `SagaExecution.current_count` == 1, and attempting a second saga returns `BulkheadFull` or queues.
8. All evidence entries contain: `saga_id`, `saga_type`, `step_name`, `step_index`, `action` (forward/compensate), `result`, `trace_id`, `epoch_id`.

### Teardown
1. Drop the `SagaOrchestrator` and backing store.
2. Verify no leaked leases in `LeaseStore`.
3. Verify bulkhead counts are zero.

---

## Structured Logging Fields

### `SagaStepEvent` (emitted for every saga step, forward or compensate)
| Field | Type | Example | Required |
|-------|------|---------|----------|
| `timestamp` | `DeterministicTimestamp` | `1708444800000000` | yes |
| `trace_id` | `TraceId` | `"a1b2c3d4..."` | yes |
| `component` | `&'static str` | `"saga_orchestrator"` | yes |
| `event_type` | `&'static str` | `"saga_step"` | yes |
| `outcome` | `Outcome` | `"success"` / `"failed"` / `"compensated"` | yes |
| `error_code` | `Option<ErrorCode>` | `"FE-8003"` | if failed |
| `saga_id` | `SagaId` | `"saga-q-001"` | yes |
| `saga_type` | `&'static str` | `"quarantine"` | yes |
| `step_name` | `&str` | `"propagate_quarantine"` | yes |
| `step_index` | `u32` | `2` | yes |
| `action` | `SagaAction` enum | `"forward"` / `"compensate"` | yes |
| `idempotency_key` | `IdempotencyKey` | `"idem-q-001-step-2"` | yes |
| `lease_id` | `LeaseId` | `"lease-001"` | yes |
| `epoch_id` | `SecurityEpoch` | `7` | yes |
| `duration_ms` | `u64` | `45` | yes |

### `SagaLifecycleEvent` (emitted on saga state transitions: Created, Completed, Failed)
| Field | Type | Example | Required |
|-------|------|---------|----------|
| `timestamp` | `DeterministicTimestamp` | `1708444800000000` | yes |
| `trace_id` | `TraceId` | `"a1b2c3d4..."` | yes |
| `component` | `&'static str` | `"saga_orchestrator"` | yes |
| `event_type` | `&'static str` | `"saga_lifecycle"` | yes |
| `outcome` | `Outcome` | `"created"` / `"completed"` / `"failed"` | yes |
| `saga_id` | `SagaId` | `"saga-q-001"` | yes |
| `saga_type` | `&'static str` | `"quarantine"` | yes |
| `total_steps` | `u32` | `4` | yes |
| `completed_steps` | `u32` | `2` | yes |
| `compensated_steps` | `u32` | `2` | yes |
| `failure_reason` | `Option<String>` | `"remote_unavailable"` | if failed |

---

## Implementation Approach Clarification

### Module Placement
- `src/saga/orchestrator.rs` — `SagaOrchestrator`, execution loop, crash recovery
- `src/saga/definition.rs` — `Saga`, `SagaStep`, `SagaState`, `SagaType`
- `src/saga/workflows.rs` — `QuarantineSaga`, `RevocationSaga`, `EvictionSaga`, `PublishSaga` definitions
- `src/saga/store.rs` — `SagaStore` trait, durable persistence

### Core Data Structures
```
pub struct Saga {
    saga_id: SagaId,
    saga_type: SagaType,
    steps: Vec<SagaStep>,
    state: SagaState,
    created_at: DeterministicTimestamp,
    epoch_id: SecurityEpoch,
    trace_id: TraceId,
}

pub enum SagaState {
    Pending,
    InProgress { step_index: u32 },
    Compensating { step_index: u32 },
    Completed,
    Failed { diagnostic: String, compensated_through: u32 },
}
```

### Crash Recovery Algorithm
On startup: `SagaStore::list_in_progress()` returns all sagas not in terminal state (`Completed` / `Failed`). For each:
- If `InProgress(n)`: step `n` may have partially executed. Re-execute step `n` using its idempotency key (guarantees at-most-once semantics). Continue forward from step `n`.
- If `Compensating(n)`: compensation may have partially executed for step `n`. Re-execute compensation for step `n` using its idempotency key. Continue compensation backward.

### Builder Pattern for Saga Definition
```
let quarantine = SagaBuilder::new("quarantine")
    .step("suspend_extension", compensate: "resume_extension")
    .step("flush_evidence", compensate: "noop")
    .step("propagate_quarantine", compensate: "retract_quarantine")
    .step("confirm_quarantine", compensate: "noop")
    .build();
```

title: [10.15] Add frankensqlite-backed lineage/evidence index for replacement receipts and deterministic replay joins.
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.15 (Delta Moonshots Execution Track), subsection 9I.6 (Verified Self-Replacement Architecture), item 7 of 8.

## What
Add a frankensqlite-backed lineage/evidence index for replacement receipts and deterministic replay joins.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Storage schema:
   - **Replacement receipts table**: stores full replacement_receipt artifacts indexed by slot_id, old_cell_digest, new_cell_digest, promotion timestamp, and receipt content hash.
   - **Demotion receipts table**: stores demotion_receipt artifacts with the same indexing plus demotion_reason classification.
   - **Evidence index**: maps receipt IDs to their associated validation artifacts (gate results, benchmarks, adversarial test results, divergence diagnostics).
   - **Lineage chain index**: ordered sequence of replacements per slot for efficient lineage traversal.
2. Replay-join support:
   - Queries joining replacement events with: gate results, performance benchmarks, sentinel risk scores, and differential execution logs.
   - Support time-range queries for operational dashboards.
3. Deterministic retrieval:
   - Identical query inputs produce identical result ordering.
   - Content-addressable lookups for individual receipts.
4. Performance requirements:
   - Lineage query for a single slot: sub-millisecond at expected slot counts.
   - Cross-slot aggregate queries (e.g., native coverage): bounded latency.
5. Schema migration support for evolving receipt formats.
6. All storage operations use /dp/frankensqlite integration patterns.

## Rationale
From 10.15: "Add frankensqlite-backed lineage/evidence index for replacement receipts and deterministic replay joins." Persistent indexed storage of replacement evidence is required for: operator dashboards (fast queries), verifier CLI (lineage traversal), audit (evidence joins), and the GA release gate (native coverage verification).

## Testing Requirements
- Unit tests: CRUD operations, index query correctness, replay-join correctness, deterministic retrieval.
- Conformance tests: round-trip fidelity, schema migration, concurrent access.
- Performance tests: latency benchmarks at target data volumes.

## Implementation Notes
- Use /dp/frankensqlite; consider /dp/sqlmodel_rust for typed model layers.
- Index design should optimize for the query patterns used by the operator dashboard (bd-3sq4) and verifier CLI (bd-kr99).
- Consider materialized views for frequently queried aggregates (e.g., native coverage percentage).

## Dependencies
- bd-7rwi (replacement_receipt and related schemas).
- bd-27i1 (demotion_receipt schema).
- 10.14 (frankensqlite integration patterns).
- /dp/frankensqlite (storage framework).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Implement the full objective with deterministic behavior, explicit failure semantics, and safe fallback/rollback rules.
- Add focused unit tests for normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid or adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
- Add integration and/or end-to-end test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions, degraded mode, and recovery behavior with deterministic fixtures.
- Emit structured logs with stable keys (trace_id, decision_id, policy_id, component, event, outcome, error_code) and assert critical events in tests.
- Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, evidence pointers, replay pointers, benchmark/check outputs) plus clear operator verification steps.
- Ensure heavy Rust build/test execution paths are documented and run through rch wrappers when implementation begins.

description:
## Plan Reference
Section 15: Ecosystem Capture Strategy.

## What
Adoption-strategy epic that converts technical superiority into ecosystem-scale uptake through migration pathways, governance integrations, trust APIs, and partner proof points.

## Rationale
Technical strength without adoption infrastructure does not create category displacement. This epic ensures FrankenEngine’s differentiated capabilities become operationally and commercially consumable for real organizations.

## Scope and Boundaries
In scope:
- signed registry and provenance/revocation governance surfaces
- migration kits and deterministic validation for incumbent workloads
- enterprise governance/compliance integration patterns
- ecosystem trust/reputation interfaces and lighthouse partner program

Out of scope:
- performance/security claim publication without section-14 validation
- adoption claims lacking concrete case-study evidence

## Dependency Model
This epic depends on validated program claims (sections 13 and 14) and implementation completion from section 10.x. It provides prerequisite outcomes for section-16 scientific/industry impact targets.

## Validation Model
- Adoption artifacts must be testable, reproducible, and user-operable.
- Migration and onboarding flows require deterministic validation evidence.
- Structured operational evidence must back case-study and partner claims.

## Success Criteria
1. All child ecosystem beads close with actionable adoption artifacts.
2. Migration/onboarding workflows are deterministic and evidence-backed.
3. Enterprise governance and trust-sharing surfaces are production-viable.
4. Section output materially increases adoption velocity and trust posture.

title: [10.15] Add frankentui operator surfaces for proof-specialization lineage (`proof ids`, `activated specializations`, `invalidations`, `fallback events`).
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.15 (Delta Moonshots Execution Track), subsection 9I.8 (Security-Proof-Guided Specialization), item 3 of 4.

## What
Add frankentui operator surfaces for proof-specialization lineage showing proof IDs, activated specializations, invalidations, and fallback events.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Dashboard views:
   - **Proof inventory**: table of active security proofs (capability_witnesses, flow_proofs, replay_motifs) with validity status, epoch, and linked specializations count.
   - **Active specializations**: per-extension or per-slot view of currently activated proof-grounded specializations with optimization class, performance delta, and proof references.
   - **Invalidation feed**: chronological view of specialization invalidations (epoch changes, proof expirations, proof revocations) with automatic fallback confirmations.
   - **Fallback events**: log of cases where specialization could not be applied (proof unavailable, expired, or validation failed) with the unspecialized path being used instead.
2. Interactive features:

title: [10.2] Implement closure and lexical scope model.
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.2, item 11. Cross-refs: 9I.7 (IFC flow-label propagation through scope chains), 9F.4 (Capability-Typed TS Execution), Phase A exit gate.

## What
Implement the closure and lexical scope model for ES2020, including lexical scoping, closures, block scope (let/const), hoisting, the scope chain, and the interaction between scope semantics and IFC flow analysis.

## Detailed Requirements
- Lexical scoping: function scope, block scope (let/const/class), global scope, module scope
- Closures: functions capture their enclosing lexical environment by reference; captured variables remain live as long as the closure exists
- Block scoping: let and const declarations are block-scoped with temporal dead zone (TDZ) enforcement
- Hoisting: var declarations hoisted to function scope, function declarations hoisted to function scope with initialization, let/const/class enter TDZ
- Scope chain: variable lookup traverses enclosing scopes in lexical order
- with statement: creates a dynamic scope entry (rare but must be supported for full ES2020)
- eval: direct eval runs in the calling scope, indirect eval runs in global scope
- arguments object: mapped arguments for sloppy-mode functions, unmapped for strict mode
- IFC integration: scope chain traversal must propagate IFC flow labels - when a closure captures a variable labeled with a sensitivity class, the label flows with the captured reference (per 9I.7)

## Rationale
Closures and lexical scope are foundational to JavaScript semantics. Nearly every non-trivial extension uses closures. Block scoping with TDZ is critical for correctness with modern JS patterns (let/const). The IFC connection is architecturally important: data sensitivity labels must flow through scope chains. If a closure captures a variable carrying a 'credentials' label, any function that invokes that closure and reads the captured value must inherit the label. Without this, IFC flow analysis has a scope-chain-shaped hole that attackers could exploit.

## Testing Requirements
- Unit tests: lexical scoping - variable shadowing across nested functions
- Unit tests: closure captures - verify captured variables reflect mutations in enclosing scope
- Unit tests: block scope - let/const TDZ throws ReferenceError before declaration
- Unit tests: hoisting - var vs let/const vs function declaration behavior
- Unit tests: scope chain traversal across multiple nesting levels
- Unit tests: eval in direct and indirect modes
- Unit tests: arguments object (mapped vs unmapped)
- Unit tests: IFC label propagation through closure captures
- Conformance: test262 language/statements/let, language/statements/const, language/expressions/function, language/statements/with
- Edge cases: closure over loop variables (let in for-loop), mutual recursion through closures, deeply nested closures

## Implementation Notes
- Environment records should be arena-allocated (per 9B.1 recommendation)
- Consider environment record types: declarative, object (for with), function, global, module
- Closure representation: function code reference + captured environment chain
- TDZ enforcement: mark bindings as uninitialized until declaration is evaluated
- IFC label propagation: environment records carry label metadata that joins on capture

## Dependencies
- Blocked by: baseline interpreter skeleton (bd-2f8), ES2020 object semantics (bd-1m9) for scope objects
- Blocks: Phase A exit gate conformance, IFC flow-check accuracy (bd-3jg) for scope-aware flow analysis

title: [CRITICAL] [REVIEW] Capability witness active acceptance self-trusts embedded signer key
description:
Reality-check scope: crates/franken-engine/src/capability_witness.rs versus AGENTS.md/README/PLAN runtime-security claims.

AGENTS.md:128 says the engine mission includes mathematically explicit runtime security for untrusted extension code. README.md:50 describes capability-typed execution with ambient-authority rejection as the target posture. PLAN_TO_CREATE_FRANKEN_ENGINE.md:891-902 describes PLAS as proof-carrying least-authority synthesis with signed capability_witness artifacts consumed as live promoted snapshots.

The active witness acceptance path does not use an external trust root. capability_witness.rs:1197-1220 reads the trusted synthesizer verification key out of the witness metadata itself. WitnessBuilder::build then automatically inserts the builder signing key as trusted_synthesizer_verification_key at capability_witness.rs:1417-1423. verify_active_acceptance only verifies the synthesizer signature against that self-embedded key at capability_witness.rs:1250-1251.

The promotion signature check is also only a shape check: capability_witness.rs:1240-1248 accepts any promotion_signatures entry with length 64, and the builder fills promotion_signatures with the same synthesizer signature at capability_witness.rs:1483-1484. No promotion signer identity, quorum membership, or external policy root is verified.

Impact: an arbitrary local signer can build a witness that carries its own verification key and can satisfy active-acceptance signature checks. That undercuts the documented signed promoted snapshot / least-authority runtime-security boundary.

Acceptance: active/publishable witness verification must resolve trusted synthesizer and promotion quorum keys from an external pinned trust root or policy artifact, verify every required promotion signature against authorized keys, and reject self-embedded trust anchors unless explicitly tied to a verified trust-chain artifact.
close_reason: shipped: active/publishable capability witness acceptance now requires an external CapabilityWitnessTrustRoot; synthesizer and promotion signatures are verified against authorized trust-root keys instead of self-embedded witness metadata. Implemented in a2c607f0 and borrow-checker cleanup ac3956ac.

title: [10.15] Implement deterministic shadow ablation engine that tests capability subtraction candidates against correctness and risk invariants.
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.15 (Delta Moonshots Execution Track), subsection 9I.5 (PLAS), item 3 of 14.

## What
Implement the deterministic shadow ablation engine that tests capability subtraction candidates against correctness and risk invariants to find the minimal required capability set.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Ablation pipeline:
   - Start from the static upper bound (from bd-2lr7) as the initial candidate set.
   - Systematically attempt capability subtractions (removing one or more capabilities from the candidate set).
   - For each subtraction candidate, run the extension in a deterministic shadow environment and evaluate:
     - Behavioral correctness: does the extension produce correct outputs on the test/replay corpus?
     - Policy invariants: are all declared invariants maintained?
     - Risk budgets: does the reduced capability set stay within acceptable risk thresholds?
2. Ablation strategy:
   - Start with single-capability subtractions, then explore multi-capability subtractions for correlated capabilities.
   - Use binary search or lattice-guided search to minimize the number of shadow evaluations.
   - Deterministic ordering and seeding so ablation sequence is reproducible.
3. Shadow environment:
   - Isolated execution environment with capability enforcement.
   - Deterministic inputs: pinned test corpus, fixed seeds, controlled timing.
   - Full execution tracing for diagnosis of ablation-induced failures.
4. Output: per-subtraction evaluation results (pass/fail, failure detail, correctness metrics) plus final minimal capability set.
5. Search budget: configurable limits on time/compute/depth (integrates with bd-83jh budget contract).
6. All ablation runs must produce signed transcript artifacts for audit and replay.

## Rationale
From 9I.5: "Dynamic ablation pass runs staged capability subtraction experiments in deterministic shadow environments; each subtraction is evaluated against behavioral correctness, policy invariants, and risk budgets." The ablation engine is the dynamic complement to static analysis, tightening the capability envelope beyond what static analysis alone can achieve by testing actual runtime behavior.

## Testing Requirements
- Unit tests: ablation strategy correctness (search finds known minimal sets on simple examples), deterministic ordering verification.
- Integration tests: full ablation pipeline on representative extensions, verify resulting minimal set preserves correctness.
- Adversarial tests: extensions that behave differently based on capability availability (attempting to detect and circumvent ablation).
- Deterministic replay: identical ablation inputs produce identical results and transcripts.

## Implementation Notes
- Shadow environment should reuse the sandbox/containment infrastructure from 10.5.
- Consider parallelizing independent subtraction evaluations for throughput.
- Ablation transcript should feed the PLAS witness proof obligations.

## Dependencies

- bd-83jh (synthesis search-budget contract for resource limits).
- 10.5 (sandbox infrastructure for shadow execution).
- 10.7 (test corpus and conformance infrastructure for correctness evaluation).

title: [review][baseline_interpreter] Route URI component builtins through shared UTF-8 percent codec
description: Review finding from commit 0c138036 in crates/franken-engine/src/baseline_interpreter.rs. The batch-38 builtin:EncodeURIComponent and builtin:DecodeURIComponent arms read their first argument from args.start + 1 at lines 18628 and 18658, while dispatch_builtin_hostcall uses args.start as the first argument for global-style builtins. A single-argument encodeURIComponent("a b") can therefore read the next register or Undefined instead of the provided value. After that register bug is fixed, the local codec is still not compatible with JavaScript URI component semantics: EncodeURIComponent iterates Unicode scalar chars and formats c as a code point at lines 18641-18646, so non-ASCII input like emoji is emitted as a single invalid percent sequence instead of UTF-8 bytes, and DecodeURIComponent decodes each %XX byte directly into a char at lines 18677-18681 instead of reconstructing UTF-8. stdlib.rs already has byte-oriented percent_encode and percent_decode helpers; centralize baseline URI builtins on that shared codec and add regressions for both builtin IDs 373 and 374 covering single-argument dispatch, spaces, reserved characters, and multi-byte UTF-8 round trips.
close_reason: done: Routed URI component builtins through shared UTF-8 percent codec. Consolidated encodeURI/encodeURIComponent/decodeURI/decodeURIComponent through shared machinery. title: [10.15] Add compiler policy that only proof-grounded specializations may bypass capability/flow dynamic checks in marked regions.
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.15 (Delta Moonshots Execution Track), subsection 9I.8 (Security-Proof-Guided Specialization), item 2 of 4.

## What
Add a compiler policy that restricts proof-grounded specializations so only optimizations backed by valid security proofs may bypass capability or flow dynamic checks in marked regions.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Compiler policy rules:
   - **Proof-required gate**: before any specialization that elides a capability check or flow-label check, the compiler must verify that a valid, non-expired security proof covers the elided check.
   - **Proof types accepted**: PLAS capability_witness (proves capability is unreachable, so check is unnecessary), IFC flow_proof (proves flow is safe, so label check is unnecessary), replay sequence motif (proves execution pattern is stable, so fused superinstruction is sound).
   - **Validity enforcement**: proofs must be within their validity_epoch; expired proofs cannot justify specializations.
   - **Marked regions**: code regions where specialization is applied must be explicitly marked in the IR with proof references (no implicit optimization).
2. Fail-closed behavior:
   - If a proof is invalid, expired, or unavailable, the specialization is not applied and the unspecialized code path (with full dynamic checks) is used.
   - Automatic invalidation of all specializations when proof epoch changes, with re-evaluation on new proofs.
3. Receipt emission: every applied specialization emits a proof_specialization_receipt (bd-6qsi).
4. Audit trail: the compiler logs every specialization decision (applied or rejected) with structured detail.
5. Policy is configurable per optimization class with sensible defaults (conservative by default, can be relaxed per-class with governance approval).

## Rationale
From 9I.8: "PLAS capability witnesses define unreachable authority branches; optimizer specializes hostcall dispatch and removes provably unreachable paths. IFC flow proofs identify regions where label propagation/checks are unnecessary; optimizer elides those checks in proven-safe regions." and risk register: "Stale/invalid security proofs causing unsound specialization: Countermeasure: epoch-bound proof validity, mandatory specialization invalidation on proof churn, and fail-closed fallback to unspecialized paths." The compiler policy ensures that security-driven optimizations are never unsound.

## Testing Requirements
- Unit tests: policy evaluation for each proof type, validity checking, fail-closed behavior on expired/missing proofs.
- Integration tests: compilation with valid proofs (specialization applied), compilation with invalid proofs (fallback used), epoch transition with specialization invalidation.
- Conformance tests from 10.7: "specialization-conformance suite ensuring proof-specialized and unspecialized execution remain semantically equivalent across policy/proof epoch transitions."
- Adversarial tests: crafted proofs that are subtly invalid, attempt to trigger specialization without proper proof backing.

## Implementation Notes
- Integrate into the IR3/IR4 lowering pipeline from 10.2.
- Proof lookup should be efficient (cached by epoch for fast validation during compilation).
- Consider a specialization-decision log for debugging optimization behavior.

## Dependencies
- bd-6qsi (specialization receipt schema for receipt emission).
- bd-2w9w (PLAS capability_witness as proof input).
- bd-1ovk (IFC flow_proof as proof input).
