title: [10.11] Add obligation leak response policy split (lab=fatal, prod=diagnostic + scoped failover)
description:
**Plan Reference:**
Section 10.11 item 7 (Group 3: Linear-Obligation Discipline). Cross-refs: 9G.3.

**What:**
Implement differentiated response to obligation leaks: fatal error in lab/test environments, diagnostic + scoped failover in production. The key principle is that leaked obligations are bugs - in lab they crash immediately for fast feedback, in production they trigger containment while preserving service.

**Detailed Requirements:**
- Configuration-driven response mode: `ObligationLeakPolicy::Lab` (panic) vs `ObligationLeakPolicy::Prod` (diagnostic + failover)
- Lab mode: obligation leak immediately panics with full context (obligation ID, creation site, deadline, elapsed time)
- Prod mode: obligation leak emits structured diagnostic, triggers scoped failover for the affected subsystem, and continues
- Scoped failover: the subsystem that leaked enters degraded mode (reject new work, drain existing)
- All leak events are recorded as high-severity evidence entries
- Leak rate is a monitored metric; sustained leaks trigger escalation

**Rationale:**
Plan 9G.3: 'Leak detection should be fatal in lab and incident-grade in production.' This split ensures fast feedback during development (no silent bugs) while maintaining production availability (no unnecessary crashes from edge-case leaks). The diagnostic evidence makes production leaks debuggable.

**Testing Requirements:**
- Unit tests: verify lab mode panics on leak
- Unit tests: verify prod mode emits diagnostic and triggers failover without panic
- Unit tests: verify scoped failover isolates affected subsystem
- Integration test: simulate obligation leak in lab mode, verify crash with context
- Integration test: simulate obligation leak in prod mode, verify recovery
close_reason: Duplicate

title: [10.11] Define supervision tree for long-lived services with restart budgets, escalation, and monotone severity
description:
**Plan Reference:**
Section 10.11 item 8 (Group 3: Linear-Obligation Discipline, extended). Cross-refs: 9G.3.

**What:**
Define a supervision tree structure for long-lived runtime services (guardplane, policy controller, evidence ledger, scheduler) with restart budgets, escalation semantics, and monotone severity outcomes.

**Detailed Requirements:**
- Supervisor type that manages a tree of child services
- Each child has a restart budget (max N restarts in time window T)
- Exhausted restart budget triggers escalation to parent supervisor
- Severity is monotone: once a service reaches a severity level, it cannot decrease without explicit operator action
- Supervision events (start, crash, restart, escalation, shutdown) are logged as evidence
- Supports graceful shutdown propagation through the tree (uses cancel->drain->finalize protocol)
- Top-level supervisor failure triggers deterministic safe mode for the entire runtime

**Rationale:**
Long-lived services crash. Without supervision, crashes in subsidiary services can cascade unpredictably. The restart budget + escalation model ensures bounded recovery attempts before escalating to broader containment. Monotone severity prevents flapping between states, which would be operationally confusing.

**Testing Requirements:**
- Unit tests: verify restart within budget succeeds
- Unit tests: verify budget exhaustion triggers escalation
- Unit tests: verify monotone severity (cannot decrease)
- Unit tests: verify graceful shutdown propagation through tree
- Integration test: crash a child service, verify supervised restart and evidence emission

title: [10.11] Build deterministic lab runtime harness with schedule replay, virtual time, and cancellation injection
description:
**Plan Reference:**
Section 10.11 item 9 (Group 4: Deterministic Lab Runtime). Cross-refs: 9G.4, Phase A exit gate.

**What:**
Build a deterministic runtime harness for testing that provides: controlled scheduling (explicit interleaving), virtual time (no real clock dependencies), and cancellation injection (force cancel at any point). This enables reproducible testing of concurrent behavior.

**Detailed Requirements:**
- `LabRuntime` struct that replaces the real async runtime for testing
- Virtual time: all time-dependent operations use a controllable clock, not real time
- Schedule replay: given a schedule trace, reproduce the exact same interleaving of operations
- Cancellation injection: insert cancellation at specified points in the execution trace
- Fault injection: inject errors (I/O failures, timeout, resource exhaustion) at specified points
- All execution produces a deterministic trace that can be replayed
- Must support multi-task concurrent execution with controlled interleaving
- Used by frankenlab scenarios (8.4.1 references frankenlab)

**Rationale:**
Plan 9G.4: 'Build deterministic schedule/fault/cancellation exploration for critical concurrency paths.' This is the testing infrastructure that makes concurrent behavior reproducible. Without it, concurrency tests are probabilistic and flaky. The Phase A exit gate requires 'deterministic evaluator green on canonical conformance corpus' which needs this harness.

**Testing Requirements:**
- Unit tests: verify virtual time advances only when explicitly stepped
- Unit tests: verify schedule replay produces identical output for identical trace
- Unit tests: verify cancellation injection triggers at specified point
- Unit tests: verify fault injection produces expected error paths
- Meta-test: verify the harness itself is deterministic (same trace = same output, always)

title: [10.11] Add systematic interleaving explorer coverage for checkpoint/revocation/policy-update race surfaces
description:
**Plan Reference:**
Section 10.11 item 10 (Group 4: Deterministic Lab Runtime). Cross-refs: 9G.4.

**What:**
Build a systematic interleaving explorer that exhaustively or strategically explores possible interleavings of concurrent operations at race-sensitive boundaries: checkpoint updates, revocation propagation, policy updates, extension lifecycle transitions.

**Detailed Requirements:**
- Explorer generates all possible orderings (for small state spaces) or uses partial-order reduction for larger ones
- Must cover: checkpoint write racing with revocation check, policy update racing with decision execution, extension load racing with quarantine
- Each explored interleaving produces a trace that can be replayed with the lab harness
- Failures produce minimized repro traces (hierarchical delta debugging per 9B.9)
- Coverage metrics: what percentage of unique interleavings have been explored
- Integrates with CI: runs key race-surface explorations as blocking tests

**Rationale:**
Plan 9G.4: 'upgrades testing from probabilistic hope-we-hit-it to reproducible exploration of race-sensitive behaviors.' Traditional concurrent testing relies on sleep/retry heuristics. Systematic exploration finds bugs that random scheduling misses, and produces deterministic repros when bugs are found.

**Testing Requirements:**
- Unit tests: verify explorer finds known race condition in a toy concurrent system
- Unit tests: verify minimizer produces minimal repro trace from a failing exploration
- Integration test: explore checkpoint/revocation race surface, verify all interleavings pass or failures are surfaced

title: [10.11] Define mandatory evidence-ledger schema for all controller/security decisions
description:
**Plan Reference:**
Section 10.11 item 11 (Group 4, extended). Cross-refs: 9G.4, 8.4.1 (franken-evidence), Section 11.

**What:**
Define the canonical evidence-ledger schema that all controller and security decisions must use. This is the structured format for recording what was decided, why, and with what evidence.

**Detailed Requirements:**
- Evidence entry schema includes: decision_id, trace_id, policy_id, timestamp, candidates considered, constraints active, chosen action, loss rationale, witness IDs, evidence hashes
- Schema must be deterministic: same decision inputs produce same evidence entry (for replay)
- Entries must have deterministic ordering rules (candidate sort order, witness ID order)
- Bounded size policy: individual entries have max size, with truncation/reference semantics for large payloads
- Schema versioning: entries carry schema_version for forward compatibility
- Must align with franken-evidence canonical schema (8.4.1)

**Rationale:**
Plan Section 11: 'Every major subsystem proposal must include change summary, hotspot/threat evidence, EV score, expected-loss model, fallback trigger, rollout wedge, rollback command, benchmark and correctness artifacts.' The evidence-ledger schema is the runtime enforcement of this requirement. Without a mandatory schema, evidence is ad-hoc and replay-incompatible.

**Testing Requirements:**
- Unit tests: verify evidence entry creation with all required fields
- Unit tests: verify deterministic serialization (same inputs = same bytes)
- Unit tests: verify ordering rules (candidates sorted, witness IDs sorted)
- Unit tests: verify size bounds enforcement
- Unit tests: verify schema version compatibility checks

title: [10.15] Add frankentui operator surfaces for capability-delta reviews (`current`, `proposed minimal`, `escrow events`, `override rationale`) with deterministic drill playback.
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.15 (Delta Moonshots Execution Track), subsection 9I.5 (PLAS), item 9 of 14.

## What
Add frankentui operator surfaces for capability-delta reviews showing current capabilities, proposed minimal envelope, escrow events, and override rationale with deterministic drill playback.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Dashboard views:
   - **Current capability view**: per-extension display of active witness capabilities vs. manifest-declared capabilities, with over-privilege ratio highlighting.
   - **Proposed minimal view**: side-by-side comparison of current vs. PLAS-synthesized minimal envelope, with per-capability justification drill-down.
   - **Escrow event feed**: real-time and historical view of escrow/deny/grant events with filtering by extension, capability, outcome, and time range.
   - **Override rationale view**: display of emergency grants and governance overrides with signed justification and review status.
2. Deterministic drill playback:
   - Click-through from any escrow event to full decision replay (reproducing the decision context from receipt + evidence).
   - Click-through from any witness capability to the proof evidence (static analysis path, ablation result, theorem check) that justifies its inclusion.
3. Interactive features:
   - Sort/filter by over-privilege ratio, escrow frequency, grant expiry status.
   - Alert indicators for extensions with high escrow rates or pending emergency-grant reviews.
   - Batch operations for reviewing multiple witness promotions.
4. Data sourcing:
   - Pull from frankensqlite witness/index stores (bd-ami3) and receipt storage.
   - Real-time updates via event subscription where supported.
5. All frankentui surfaces must follow the /dp/frankentui integration contract from 10.14.

## Rationale
From 9I.5 / 10.15: "Add frankentui operator surfaces for capability-delta reviews (current, proposed minimal, escrow events, override rationale) with deterministic drill playback." Operator surfaces make PLAS governance visible and actionable. Without them, capability policy management remains opaque and operators cannot effectively review or intervene in synthesis decisions.

## Testing Requirements
- Unit tests: data transformation and display logic for each view, filter/sort correctness.
- Integration tests: end-to-end from witness/receipt data through frankentui rendering, verify drill playback reproduces correct decision context.
- Usability tests: verify key operator workflows (review witness promotion, investigate escrow spike, approve/reject override) are completable.

## Implementation Notes
- Build on frankentui widget/layout patterns from /dp/frankentui.
- Drill playback should reuse the replay tooling from 10.5/10.12.
- Consider lazy-loading for large escrow event histories.

## Dependencies
- bd-ami3 (frankensqlite witness/index stores for data).
- bd-17v2 (receipt storage for escrow events).
- bd-2w9w (witness schema for capability data).
- 10.14 (frankentui integration patterns).
- /dp/frankentui (TUI framework).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Implement the full objective with deterministic behavior, explicit failure semantics, and safe fallback/rollback rules.
- Add focused unit tests for normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid or adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
- Add integration and/or end-to-end test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions, degraded mode, and recovery behavior with deterministic fixtures.
- Emit structured logs with stable keys (trace_id, decision_id, policy_id, component, event, outcome, error_code) and assert critical events in tests.
- Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, evidence pointers, replay pointers, benchmark/check outputs) plus clear operator verification steps.
- Ensure heavy Rust build/test execution paths are documented and run through rch wrappers when implementation begins.

title: [10.11] Define supervision tree for long-lived services with restart budgets, escalation, and monotone severity outcomes.
description:
## Plan Reference
- **Section**: 10.11 item 8 (FrankenSQLite-Inspired Runtime Systems Track)
- **9G Cross-ref**: 9G.2 — Cancellation as protocol + 9G.3 — Linear-obligation discipline
- **Top-10 Links**: #2 (Probabilistic Guardplane), #8 (Per-extension resource budget)

## What
Define a supervision tree for long-lived runtime services with restart budgets, escalation semantics, and monotone severity outcomes. This provides structured fault recovery for all persistent subsystems (policy controller, evidence flusher, remote operation manager, scheduler, sentinel) so that transient failures are recovered automatically while persistent failures escalate deterministically.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Define a \`Supervisor\` type that manages a tree of child \`Service\` instances, each with:
   - \`service_id\`: unique, stable identifier.
   - \`restart_policy\`: one of \`Permanent\` (always restart), \`Transient\` (restart on unexpected failure only), \`Temporary\` (never restart).
   - \`restart_budget\`: \`RestartBudget { max_restarts: u32, window: Duration }\` — maximum restarts within a sliding window.
   - \`shutdown_order\`: numeric priority for ordered shutdown (higher = shut down first).
2. Restart budget enforcement: when a service exhausts its restart budget, the supervisor escalates to its parent supervisor. Escalation is monotone: severity only increases (restart -> isolate -> parent restart -> terminate subtree).
3. Monotone severity outcomes: define a \`Severity\` enum: \`Restart < Isolate < SubtreeRestart < SubtreeTerminate < RootEscalation\`. Severity transitions must be monotonically non-decreasing within a single incident chain.
4. Each service restart must follow the region-quiescence protocol (bd-2ao): the old instance is \`cancel -> drain -> finalize\`d before the new instance starts. This prevents overlapping service instances.
5. Supervision tree structure must be declarative: defined at startup via configuration, not ad-hoc runtime construction.
6. All supervisor actions emit structured evidence events: \`service_id\`, \`action\` (start/restart/isolate/terminate/escalate), \`reason\`, \`restart_count\`, \`budget_remaining\`, \`severity\`, \`trace_id\`.
7. Health reporting: each supervisor node reports aggregate health (\`healthy\`, \`degraded\`, \`critical\`) based on child states and restart budget utilization.
8. Integration with obligation leak policy (bd-qse): an obligation leak in a service triggers the supervisor to handle the failure according to the service's restart policy.

## Rationale
Long-lived runtime services fail in production. Without structured supervision, failures cascade unpredictably: a crashed policy controller might leave stale decisions active, a crashed evidence flusher might lose audit entries. The supervision tree (inspired by Erlang/OTP and adapted for the FrankenEngine safety model) ensures that failures are contained, recovery is bounded, and escalation is deterministic. Monotone severity prevents oscillation (restart loops) and ensures that persistent failures are surfaced to operators, not hidden by infinite retries.

## Testing Requirements
- **Unit tests**: Verify restart budget enforcement (service restarts within budget, exhaustion triggers escalation). Verify monotone severity (severity never decreases within an incident chain). Verify shutdown ordering.
- **Property tests**: Randomly inject failures into a supervision tree and verify: (a) budget accounting is correct, (b) severity is monotone, (c) no service instance overlap (old finalized before new starts), (d) escalation reaches root if all budgets exhausted.
- **Integration tests**: Build a 3-level supervision tree, inject repeated failures at leaf level, verify escalation propagates correctly and evidence events are emitted at each level.
- **Deterministic replay test**: Record a supervision failure/recovery sequence in the lab runtime, replay it, and verify identical event sequence.
- **Logging/observability**: All supervisor actions emit structured events with the fields specified in requirement 6.

## Implementation Notes
- Model after Erlang/OTP supervisor patterns but adapted for async Rust with \`tokio\` task management.
- Services should implement a \`Service\` trait with \`start(cx: Cx) -> Result<ServiceHandle>\` and \`health() -> HealthStatus\`.
- Use the region-quiescence protocol (bd-2ao) for service lifecycle management.
- The supervision tree configuration should be serializable for inclusion in reproducibility artifacts.

## Dependencies
- Depends on: bd-2ao (region-quiescence for service restart lifecycle), bd-qse (obligation leak triggers supervisor action), bd-1i2 (capability profiles for service context).
- Blocks: bd-121 (lab runtime uses supervision for test service management), bd-1si (PolicyController is a supervised service), bd-gr1 (regime detector is a supervised service).

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Implement the full objective with explicit deterministic behavior, failure semantics, and rollback constraints where applicable.
2. Add focused unit tests covering normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid or adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
3. Add end-to-end or integration test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions and failure recovery paths using deterministic seeds or fixtures and CI-ready command lines.
4. Emit structured logs with stable fields (trace_id, decision_id, policy_id, component, event, outcome, error_code) and add assertions for critical log events in tests.
5. Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, replay/evidence pointers, benchmark/check outputs) and document operator verification steps.
6. For Rust build or test workflows introduced by this bead, document or execute via rch-wrapped commands for heavy compilation or test workloads.

# Enrichment: Concrete E2E Test Scenario, Logging Field Specs, Implementation Approach

## Concrete E2E Test Scenario: Supervision Tree Escalation and Monotone Severity

### Setup
1. Build a 3-level supervision tree:
   - `root` supervisor (restart budget: 5 in 60s)
     - `infra` supervisor (restart budget: 3 in 30s)
       - `evidence_flusher` service (Permanent, restart budget: 2 in 10s)
       - `lease_renewer` service (Permanent, restart budget: 2 in 10s)
     - `policy` supervisor (restart budget: 3 in 30s)
       - `policy_controller` service (Permanent, restart budget: 2 in 10s)
       - `regime_detector` service (Transient, restart budget: 1 in 10s)
     - `temp_worker` service (Temporary, restart budget: 0 — never restart)
2. Set up a mock `RegionQuiescence` protocol for service lifecycle.
3. Set up a mock `ObligationLeakDetector` (bd-qse) that can inject leak events.
4. Create an evidence capture sink for supervisor events.

### Exercise
1. **Normal startup**: Start the tree. Verify: all 5 services start in order (by `shutdown_order`), health report: `healthy`.
2. **Transient failure + restart**: Inject failure into `evidence_flusher`. Verify: service is drained via `cancel -> drain -> finalize`, then restarted. Health report: `healthy` (recovered).
3. **Budget exhaustion + escalation**: Inject 3 rapid failures into `evidence_flusher` within 10s (exceeds budget of 2 in 10s). Verify:
   - First 2 failures: service restarted normally (budget: 2/2 used).
   - Third failure: `evidence_flusher` budget exhausted. Escalation to `infra` supervisor.
   - `infra` supervisor restarts its entire subtree (`evidence_flusher` + `lease_renewer`).
   - `infra` supervisor budget: 1/3 used.
4. **Monotone severity check**: After step 3, inject another failure into `evidence_flusher`. Verify:
   - `evidence_flusher` budget is reset after subtree restart.
   - This new failure uses the fresh budget (restart, not immediately escalate).
5. **Transient service expected shutdown**: Stop `regime_detector` gracefully (expected exit). Verify: NOT restarted (Transient policy — only restarts on unexpected failure).
6. **Temporary service failure**: Inject failure into `temp_worker`. Verify: NOT restarted (Temporary policy), supervisor marks it as `Terminated`.
7. **Obligation leak trigger**: Inject obligation leak into `policy_controller` via mock `ObligationLeakDetector`. Verify: supervisor handles according to restart policy (Permanent -> restart).
8. **Root escalation**: Exhaust budgets at all levels:
   - Exhaust `evidence_flusher` budget (triggers `infra` subtree restart).
   - Exhaust `infra` budget (triggers `root` subtree restart or isolation).
   - Verify: root supervisor enters `RootEscalation` severity — fatal/operator-alert.
9. **Ordered shutdown**: Trigger graceful shutdown of entire tree. Verify: services shut down in reverse `shutdown_order` (highest first).

### Assert
1. Step 1: startup order matches `shutdown_order` values (ascending).
2. Step 2: evidence event contains `action: "restart"`, `service_id: "evidence_flusher"`, `severity: "Restart"`, `restart_count: 1`, `budget_remaining: 1`.
3. Step 3: evidence events show severity escalation: `Restart(1) -> Restart(2) -> SubtreeRestart`. The `infra` supervisor's event shows `action: "subtree_restart"`, `severity: "SubtreeRestart"`.
4. Step 3: Severity values in the incident chain are monotonically non-decreasing: `Restart <= Restart <= SubtreeRestart`.
5. Step 5: No restart event for `regime_detector` after graceful shutdown.
6. Step 6: No restart event for `temp_worker` after failure.
7. Step 7: `policy_controller` restart event with `reason: "obligation_leak"`.
8. Step 8: Root escalation event with `severity: "RootEscalation"`, `action: "terminate_subtree"` or `"operator_alert"`.
9. Step 9: Shutdown order is exact reverse of startup order.
10. Health reporting: after step 3, `infra` supervisor reports `degraded` during restart, then `healthy` after recovery.
11. Total evidence events >= 15 across all steps.

### Teardown
1. Ensure all services are stopped.
2. Drop the supervision tree.
3. Verify no leaked tasks or channels.

---

## Structured Logging Fields

### `SupervisorActionEvent`

| `timestamp` | `DeterministicTimestamp` | `1708444800000000` | yes |
| `trace_id` | `TraceId` | `"a1b2c3d4..."` | yes |

| `error_code` | `Option<ErrorCode>` | `"FE-8001"` | if escalation |
| `supervisor_id` | `&str` | `"infra"` | yes |

| `action` | `SupervisorAction` enum | `"restart"` / `"subtree_restart"` / `"terminate"` / `"escalate"` | yes |

## Implementation Approach Clarification

### Module Placement
- `src/supervision/tree.rs` — `SupervisionTree`, tree builder, declarative config
- `src/supervision/supervisor.rs` — `Supervisor`, restart logic, escalation
- `src/supervision/service.rs` — `Service` trait, `ServiceHandle`, lifecycle
- `src/supervision/severity.rs` — `Severity` enum with `Ord` impl for monotonicity
- `src/supervision/mod.rs` — re-exports

### Core Data Structures
```
pub struct Supervisor {
    id: String,
    children: Vec<SupervisedChild>,
    restart_budget: RestartBudget,
    parent: Option<Arc<Supervisor>>,
    health: AtomicHealth,
}

pub enum SupervisedChild {
    Service(ServiceEntry),
    Supervisor(Arc<Supervisor>),
}

pub struct ServiceEntry {
    service_id: String,
    restart_policy: RestartPolicy,
    restart_budget: RestartBudget,
    shutdown_order: u32,
    current_instance: Option<ServiceHandle>,
    restart_history: VecDeque<DeterministicTimestamp>,  // sliding window
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
pub enum Severity {
    Restart = 0,
    Isolate = 1,
    SubtreeRestart = 2,
    SubtreeTerminate = 3,
    RootEscalation = 4,
}
```

### Monotone Severity Enforcement
Each incident chain carries a `max_severity: Severity` field. When escalating, the new severity must be `>= max_severity`. This is enforced by the `Supervisor::escalate` method which compares `Severity::ord()`. Violation is a programming error caught by `debug_assert!`.

### Restart Budget Sliding Window
```
fn is_budget_exhausted(&self) -> bool {
    let now = deterministic_now();
    let window_start = now - self.restart_budget.window;
    let recent_restarts = self.restart_history.iter()
        .filter(|t| **t >= window_start)
        .count();
    recent_restarts >= self.restart_budget.max_restarts as usize
}
```

### Service Lifecycle Integration
Each service restart follows: (1) `cancel` old instance via `CancellationToken`, (2) `drain` pending work (wait up to drain_timeout), (3) `finalize` cleanup (release obligations, flush buffers), (4) `start` new instance. This is the bd-2ao region-quiescence protocol applied to individual services.

### Declarative Configuration
```
let tree = SupervisionTree::builder()
    .supervisor("root", budget(5, 60))
        .supervisor("infra", budget(3, 30))
            .service("evidence_flusher", Permanent, budget(2, 10), shutdown_order: 10)
            .service("lease_renewer", Permanent, budget(2, 10), shutdown_order: 20)
        .end()
        .supervisor("policy", budget(3, 30))
            .service("policy_controller", Permanent, budget(2, 10), shutdown_order: 30)
            .service("regime_detector", Transient, budget(1, 10), shutdown_order: 40)
        .end()
        .service("temp_worker", Temporary, budget(0, 0), shutdown_order: 50)
    .end()
    .build();
```

title: [10.5] Implement containment actions (`sandbox`, `suspend`, `terminate`, `quarantine`).
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.5, item 6 (Implement containment actions: sandbox, suspend, terminate, quarantine). Cross-refs: 9A.8 (resource budgets per extension), Phase B exit gate (median detection-to-containment <= 250ms), 9G.2 (cancellation as protocol).

## What
Implement the four containment actions that the expected-loss action selector (bd-1y5) can trigger, plus the `Allow` and `Challenge` pass-through actions. Each containment action is a deterministic operation on an extension's lifecycle state (bd-1hu) with specific resource, capability, and communication implications. The containment subsystem must meet the Phase B exit gate of median detection-to-containment latency <= 250ms, meaning from the moment the Guardplane decides to contain an extension to the moment the containment is effective, no more than 250ms may elapse (at median).

## Detailed Requirements
- Implement `ContainmentExecutor` trait with method `execute(action: ContainmentAction, target: ExtensionId, context: ContainmentContext) -> Result<ContainmentReceipt, ContainmentError>`.
- **Sandbox**: Restrict the extension's capability set to a minimal safe subset (e.g., deny all network, deny fs_write, allow only fs_read to a quarantine directory). The extension continues running but with reduced authority. Must not require extension cooperation. Implemented by intercepting hostcalls and filtering against the sandbox policy.
- **Suspend**: Pause all execution of the extension. No hostcalls are processed. Timers are frozen. The extension's state is preserved in memory for potential resume. Implemented by suspending the extension's task/fiber and draining its hostcall queue.
- **Terminate**: Initiate cooperative shutdown per 9G.2: send cancel token, wait for grace period (configurable, default 5s), then force-kill if not exited. Release all resources (memory, file handles, network connections). Log final resource accounting.
- **Quarantine**: Like terminate, but additionally: preserve the extension's memory snapshot and hostcall log for forensic analysis (bd-t2m). Mark the extension's manifest as quarantined in the trust registry. Emit a quarantine event to the supply-chain trust fabric (9A.5).
- **Allow**: No-op pass-through; log the decision for audit trail.
- **Challenge**: Request additional authentication/attestation from the extension before allowing continued operation. If the challenge is not answered within a timeout, escalate to Sandbox.
- Each containment action must produce a `ContainmentReceipt` struct: `{ receipt_id: ReceiptId, action: ContainmentAction, target: ExtensionId, timestamp_ns: u64, duration_ns: u64, success: bool, evidence_refs: Vec<EvidenceRef> }`.
- Latency budget: median execution time for any containment action <= 200ms (leaving 50ms for decision pipeline).
- All containment actions must be idempotent: executing the same action twice on an already-contained extension is a no-op returning the existing receipt.

## Rationale
Containment is the enforcement arm of the security decision system. Without fast, reliable containment, the Bayesian detection and decision components are academic exercises. The 250ms Phase B exit gate ensures that the engine can respond to threats in near-real-time. The differentiated actions (sandbox vs. suspend vs. terminate vs. quarantine) enable proportional response: the engine does not terminate an extension it could safely sandbox. Quarantine's forensic preservation is essential for post-incident analysis and for improving the Bayesian models over time.

## Testing Requirements
- **Unit tests**: Each containment action transitions the extension to the correct lifecycle state. Sandbox correctly restricts capabilities (denied hostcalls return `Denied`). Suspend freezes execution (no hostcalls processed during suspension). Terminate follows cooperative shutdown protocol. Quarantine preserves memory snapshot.
- **Latency tests**: Benchmark each containment action; assert median < 200ms. Test under load (multiple extensions being contained simultaneously).
- **Idempotency tests**: Execute each action twice on the same extension; verify second execution returns existing receipt without side effects.
- **Integration tests**: Full pipeline: telemetry -> posterior update -> action selection -> containment execution. Verify end-to-end detection-to-containment latency < 250ms.
- **Adversarial tests**: Extension that ignores cancel token (terminate must force-kill after grace period). Extension that floods hostcalls during containment (sandbox must filter correctly under load).

## Implementation Notes
- Sandbox is implemented at the hostcall dispatch layer: a `SandboxPolicy` filter is inserted into the extension's hostcall path, rejecting calls outside the allowed set.
- Suspend is implemented by pausing the extension's async task (e.g., using a `tokio::sync::Notify` gate or cooperative yield point).
- Terminate follows the 9G.2 protocol: `CancellationToken` -> grace period -> forced drop.
- Quarantine must capture the extension's memory region before termination; this may require a copy-on-write snapshot or a pre-termination memory dump.
- Receipt generation must be atomic with action execution to avoid partial containment without receipt.

## Dependencies
- **Blocked by**: bd-1hu (lifecycle manager provides state machine), bd-1y5 (action selector decides which containment to apply), bd-5pk (telemetry for logging containment events).
- **Blocks**: bd-t2m (forensic replay uses quarantine snapshots), bd-375 (delegate cells need same containment actions).
- **Parent**: bd-1yq (10.5 epic).

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Implement the full objective with explicit deterministic behavior, failure semantics, and rollback constraints where applicable.
2. Add focused unit tests covering normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid/adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
3. Add end-to-end/integration test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions and failure recovery paths using deterministic seeds/fixtures and CI-ready command lines.
4. Emit structured logs with stable fields (`trace_id`, `decision_id`, `policy_id`, `component`, `event`, `outcome`, `error_code`) and add assertions for critical log events in tests.
5. Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, replay/evidence pointers, benchmark/check outputs) and document operator verification steps.
6. For Rust build/test workflows introduced by this bead, document/execute via `rch`-wrapped commands for heavy compilation/test workloads.

title: bd-CALLER-CONVERSION-1: Convert one call site to use typed store operations
description:

title: [10.11] Add optional MMR-style compact proof support for marker-stream inclusion/prefix verification.
description:
## Plan Reference
- **Section**: 10.11 item 29 (FrankenSQLite-Inspired Runtime Systems Track)
- **9G Cross-ref**: 9G.9 — Three-tier integrity strategy + append-only decision stream
- **Top-10 Links**: #3 (Deterministic evidence graph + replay), #10 (Provenance + revocation fabric)

## What
Add optional MMR-style (Merkle Mountain Range) compact proof support for marker-stream inclusion and prefix verification. This enables efficient cryptographic proofs that a specific decision marker exists in the stream and that the stream prefix up to a given point is consistent.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Implement a \`MerkleMountainRange\` data structure over the decision marker stream (bd-3e7):
   - Append-only: new markers are appended as leaves.
   - Peaks: maintains a set of peaks (complete binary tree roots) that compactly represent the entire stream.
   - Root hash: a single root hash derived from the peaks that commits to the entire stream state.
2. Proof types:
   - **Inclusion proof**: given a marker index, produce a compact proof (O(log n) hashes) that the marker is included in the stream at the claimed position. Verifier can check the proof against the root hash without the full stream.
   - **Prefix consistency proof**: given two root hashes (old and new), produce a proof that the new stream is an append-only extension of the old stream (no markers were modified or removed).
3. Proof format: proofs are serializable structures containing: \`proof_type\`, \`marker_index\`, \`proof_hashes\` (ordered list), \`root_hash\`, \`stream_length\`, \`epoch_id\`.
4. Verification API:
   - \`verify_inclusion(marker_hash, marker_index, proof, root_hash) -> Result<(), ProofError>\`.
   - \`verify_consistency(old_root, new_root, proof) -> Result<(), ProofError>\`.
5. Compact representation: the MMR peaks enable efficient stream summarization without storing the full tree. Peak set size is O(log n) of stream length.
6. Cross-node verification: proofs can be exchanged between nodes to verify that they share a consistent view of the decision history without transmitting the full stream.
7. Integration with signed checkpoints: periodic checkpoint markers in the decision stream (bd-3e7) include the MMR root hash, binding the hash chain to the MMR commitment.

## Rationale
The hash chain in the decision marker stream (bd-3e7) provides tamper evidence but requires full chain traversal for verification. MMR proofs enable efficient spot-checks: a remote node can verify that a specific decision exists in the stream, or that two nodes share a consistent stream prefix, using O(log n) data instead of O(n). This is essential for the distributed anti-entropy reconciliation (bd-2n6) and for external audit tooling that needs to verify specific decisions without downloading the entire stream. This directly supports Section 3.2 item 9 (distributed anti-entropy trust reconciliation with machine-verifiable repair artifacts).

## Testing Requirements
- **Unit tests**: Verify MMR append produces correct peaks. Verify inclusion proof generation and verification. Verify consistency proof generation and verification. Verify proof rejection for tampered data.
- **Property tests**: Append random marker sequences, generate proofs for random indices, and verify all proofs succeed. Tamper with random markers and verify proofs fail.
- **Integration tests**: Build an MMR over a real decision marker stream, generate inclusion proofs for specific decisions, and verify them against the root hash. Generate consistency proofs between stream snapshots.
- **Cross-node tests**: Simulate two nodes with the same stream, exchange proofs, and verify consistency. Simulate a divergent stream and verify consistency proof failure.
- **Performance tests**: Verify proof generation is O(log n) and verification is O(log n).

## Implementation Notes
- Use a standard MMR algorithm (e.g., from the Grin/Mimblewimble implementation lineage, adapted for Rust).
- Hash function: Tier 2 ContentHash (BLAKE3) from bd-4hf for tree hashing.
- MMR state (peaks) should be persisted alongside the marker stream in frankensqlite.
- Consider lazy peak computation: peaks are updated on append but full tree is not materialized.
- Proofs should be compact enough to include in evidence entries and network messages.

## Dependencies
- Depends on: bd-3e7 (decision marker stream provides the data to build the MMR over), bd-4hf (Tier 2 hash for tree hashing).
- Blocks: bd-2n6 (anti-entropy reconciliation uses MMR proofs for consistency verification), bd-2j3 (proof-carrying recovery artifacts may include MMR proofs).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Implement the full objective with deterministic behavior, explicit failure semantics, and safe fallback/rollback rules.
- Add focused unit tests for normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid or adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
- Add integration and/or end-to-end test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions, degraded mode, and recovery behavior with deterministic fixtures.
- Emit structured logs with stable keys (trace_id, decision_id, policy_id, component, event, outcome, error_code) and assert critical events in tests.
- Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, evidence pointers, replay pointers, benchmark/check outputs) plus clear operator verification steps.
- Ensure heavy Rust build/test execution paths are documented and run through rch wrappers when implementation begins.

title: [CRITICAL] [REVIEW] Evidence replay gate can pass without a decision replay evaluator
description:
Review finding from proof/evidence mock-stub sweep.

`EvidenceReplayChecker::replay` accepts `replay_fn: Option<&DecisionReplayFn>` and treats `None` as structural-only validation. If the chain/hash/schema checks pass, `ReplayResult.passed` and `ReplayEvidenceArtifact.gate_passed` become true even though no decision contract was re-evaluated. The docs at `crates/franken-engine/src/evidence_replay_checker.rs:207-212` say production should call the actual decision contract, but the primary result fields do not distinguish structural-only from decision-replayed proof.

This leaks into production/release gating: `crates/franken-engine/src/release_gate.rs:620-675` builds canonical replay entries and calls `checker.replay(&replay_entries, None)`, then passes the evidence replay gate when `violations.is_empty()`. That means release evidence can claim replay success without exercising decision outcome determinism. `migration_compatibility.rs:626-635` also uses structural-only replay, which may be valid for migration checks but should be explicitly labeled as structural.

Why this matters: AGENTS.md requires significant claims to have reproducible artifacts. Decision replay proof is a significant claim; structural hash validation alone must not be emitted as a passing decision-replay proof.

Acceptance criteria:
- Split structural ledger validation from decision-outcome replay in the public API/result model.
- Release evidence replay must require a real `DecisionReplayFn` or fail/downgrade with an explicit `decision_replay_evaluator_missing` diagnostic.
- `ReplayManifest`/`ReplayEvidenceArtifact` must record whether decision replay was executed and how many entries were outcome-checked.
- Migration compatibility may keep structural-only replay only if the result/manifest names it as structural validation, not decision replay.
- Add regressions proving `replay_and_collect(..., None)` cannot produce a CI/operator artifact that looks like full decision replay success.
- Focused validation: cargo test -p frankenengine-engine evidence_replay_checker --lib plus the release_gate evidence replay tests, isolated CARGO_TARGET_DIR.

title: Governance subsystems lack a central RuntimeContext: each integrator must remember to call set_budget_enforcer on every subsystem (GcCollector, LaneScheduler, …) — composition gap
description:
Phase 3 modes-of-reasoning analysis — F7 Systems-Thinking lens.

## The architectural seam

Multiple subsystems independently expose `set_budget_enforcer(BudgetEnforcer)` setters:
- `GcCollector::set_budget_enforcer` (`gc.rs:446`)
- `LaneScheduler::set_budget_enforcer` (`scheduler_lane.rs:341`)
- (per bd-1lsy.7.25.2 follow-up) module loader, specialization admission, and others are planned

Each is wired by the eventual integrator. There is no `RuntimeContext` / `EngineWorld` struct that owns the BudgetEnforcer and threads it to each subsystem at construction. As more subsystems get budget integration, the integrator must remember every one. Forget one and the corresponding governance dimension silently no-ops (matches bd-38uej: scheduler_lane field set but never consulted).

## The bigger picture

This is the Class 7 \"composition\" gap from the deadlock-finder taxonomy: state shared across subsystems must either be (a) owned by one place and threaded explicitly, or (b) discovered at runtime via a central registry. Today it is neither — each subsystem owns its OWN `Option<BudgetEnforcer>` field, and there is no reflection or assertion that the same enforcer instance is wired everywhere.

Adjacent symptom: the swarm has been independently rediscovering and fixing missing wirings (bd-38uej, the AllocationFailed/CollectionFailed mapping omissions in error_code.rs). All trace back to the same root: no central composition root.

## Suggested fix

(a) Introduce a `pub struct EngineRuntimeContext { budget_enforcer: BudgetEnforcer, ... }` whose constructor takes a single BudgetEnforcer and produces wired subsystems via builder methods (e.g., `ctx.gc_collector(...)`, `ctx.lane_scheduler(...)`). Removes the per-subsystem setter API surface.
(b) Lighter alternative: keep setters but add a `#[must_use_or_set\"budget_enforcer\"]` lint via a custom clippy rule or a runtime debug-assert that fires at first `enforce()` time if any subsystem in the wiring graph is unwired. Too cute; skip.

Recommend (a) as bd-1lsy.7.25.2's natural completion: one composition root, no integrator footguns.

## Severity

MEDIUM — currently latent; fires as missing-wiring bugs (bd-38uej style) that the swarm catches reactively. Becomes HIGH once production wiring exists and each silent omission is a compliance gap.
close_reason: Added GovernanceContext composition root (governance_context.rs, 277 lines + 4 unit tests). Owns BudgetEnforcer and produces pre-wired GcCollector/LaneScheduler via with_gc_collector/with_lane_scheduler factories. Adding a new governance-aware subsystem now only requires extending this struct rather than auditing every integrator. Existing set_budget_enforcer setters retained for backwards compat. cargo check --lib clean (3m34s, b8l2vd4u6 exit 0). Commit 3cb9c7a8.

title: [10.10] Enforce revocation checks before token acceptance, risky operation execution, and extension activation.
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.10, item 18. Cross-refs: 9E.7 (Revocation-head freshness semantics and degraded-mode policy - "require revocation checks before token acceptance, high-risk operation execution, and connector/extension activation"), Top-10 links #5, #8, #10.

## What
Enforce mandatory revocation checks at three critical enforcement points: before accepting any capability token, before executing any high-risk operation, and before activating any extension or connector. If the target object (token, key, attestation, extension) has been revoked, the operation must be denied. Revocation checking is non-optional and cannot be bypassed.

## Detailed Requirements
- Define three enforcement points as mandatory interceptors in the runtime execution path:
  1. **Token acceptance**: before any capability token is used to authorize an action, check `is_revoked(token.jti)` and `is_revoked(token.issuer_key_id)` against the revocation chain (bd-26f)
  2. **High-risk operation execution**: before executing operations classified as high-risk (policy changes, key operations, data export, cross-zone actions), check revocation status of the requesting principal's current key attestation
  3. **Extension activation**: before loading, initializing, or resuming an extension, check `is_revoked(extension_id)` and `is_revoked(extension_signing_key_id)`
- Transitive revocation: if a key is revoked, all tokens issued by that key are implicitly revoked (without needing individual revocation entries); implement transitive lookup
- Check ordering: revocation check must happen *after* signature verification (to avoid denial-of-service on invalid objects) but *before* any state mutation or side effect
- Failure mode: revocation check failure (revoked target) must produce a hard denial with structured error: `RevocationDenial { target_type, target_id, revocation_id, enforcement_point }`
- Audit emission: every revocation check (both pass and fail) should emit a structured audit event for forensic traceability
- Performance: revocation checks are on the critical path; they must be O(1) amortized (use the index from bd-26f)
- No bypass: there must be no code path that reaches token acceptance, high-risk execution, or extension activation without passing through revocation checking; enforce via type system or mandatory middleware
- Graceful handling of revocation chain unavailability is covered by bd-1ai (freshness policy); this bead focuses on the check mechanics when the chain is available

## Rationale
From plan section 9E.7: "require revocation checks before token acceptance, high-risk operation execution, and connector/extension activation." Revocation is only effective if it is actually checked. Many systems implement revocation lists but fail to enforce checking at every relevant point, creating windows where revoked credentials remain effective. By making revocation checks mandatory interceptors at three specific enforcement points, the system ensures that no revoked credential can be used for any meaningful action. The "no bypass" requirement prevents accidental or deliberate circumvention.

## Testing Requirements
- Unit tests: accept valid (non-revoked) token, verify pass
- Unit tests: reject revoked token (by jti), verify RevocationDenial error
- Unit tests: reject token whose issuer key is revoked (transitive revocation)
- Unit tests: reject high-risk operation when requesting principal's attestation is revoked
- Unit tests: reject extension activation when extension ID is revoked
- Unit tests: reject extension activation when extension signing key is revoked
- Unit tests: verify audit event emission for both pass and fail checks
- Unit tests: verify check ordering (revocation check after signature verification)
- Integration tests: revoke a token mid-session, verify subsequent use is denied
- Integration tests: revoke an extension, verify it cannot be activated
- Integration tests: revoke an issuer key, verify all tokens from that issuer are transitively denied
- Adversarial tests: attempt to bypass revocation check via alternate code path, verify impossible (type system enforcement)

## Implementation Notes
- Implement as a `RevocationGuard` middleware/interceptor that wraps the three enforcement points
- Use Rust's type system to enforce checking: e.g., `UnverifiedToken` -> (signature check) -> `SignatureVerifiedToken` -> (revocation check) -> `FullyVerifiedToken`; only `FullyVerifiedToken` can authorize actions
- Transitive revocation lookup: maintain a secondary index from issuer key ID to all tokens issued by that key, or check issuer key status during token verification
- For high-risk operations, define a `HighRiskOperation` enum that explicitly enumerates what qualifies as high-risk
- Performance optimization: cache revocation check results with a TTL, invalidated by new revocation events

## Dependencies
- Depends on: bd-26f (revocation object chain for is_revoked queries), bd-28m (capability token format for jti and issuer fields), bd-1dp (key attestation for principal key status)
- Blocks: bd-1ai (revocation freshness policy builds on these enforcement points), bd-26o (conformance suite tests revocation enforcement)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Implement the full objective with deterministic behavior, explicit failure semantics, and safe fallback/rollback rules.
- Add focused unit tests for normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid or adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
- Add integration and/or end-to-end test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions, degraded mode, and recovery behavior with deterministic fixtures.
- Emit structured logs with stable keys (trace_id, decision_id, policy_id, component, event, outcome, error_code) and assert critical events in tests.
- Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, evidence pointers, replay pointers, benchmark/check outputs) plus clear operator verification steps.
- Ensure heavy Rust build/test execution paths are documented and run through rch wrappers when implementation begins.

comments.text:
# Enrichment: Concrete E2E Test Scenario, Logging Field Specs, Implementation Approach

## Concrete E2E Test Scenario: Revocation Enforcement Pipeline

### Setup
1. Create a `RevocationChain` with 5 seed events: revocation of `key-001`, `tok-002`, `ext-003`, `attest-004`, `key-005`.
2. Create a `RevocationGuard` middleware wired to the chain.
3. Generate a valid `CapabilityToken` (`jti: "tok-valid-001"`, issuer: `key-valid-010`, audience: `"test-verifier"`, expiry: now + 300s).
4. Generate a `CapabilityToken` (`jti: "tok-revoked-direct"`) that is directly revoked (added to chain as `tok-002`).
5. Generate a `CapabilityToken` (`jti: "tok-revoked-transitive"`, issuer: `key-001`) whose issuer key is revoked.
6. Seed an extension descriptor `ext-active-001` (not revoked) and `ext-003` (revoked).
7. Seed key attestations for principal `principal-A` (attestation: `attest-valid-001`, not revoked) and principal `principal-B` (attestation: `attest-004`, revoked).

### Exercise
1. **Token acceptance — valid**: Submit `tok-valid-001` through `RevocationGuard::check_token_acceptance()`. Expect: `Ok(FullyVerifiedToken)`.
2. **Token acceptance — directly revoked**: Submit `tok-revoked-direct`. Expect: `Err(RevocationDenial { target_type: Token, target_id: "tok-002", enforcement_point: TokenAcceptance })`.
3. **Token acceptance — transitively revoked**: Submit `tok-revoked-transitive`. Expect: `Err(RevocationDenial { target_type: Key, target_id: "key-001", enforcement_point: TokenAcceptance })`.
4. **High-risk operation — valid principal**: Execute `RevocationGuard::check_high_risk("principal-A", HighRiskOp::PolicyChange)`. Expect: `Ok(())`.
5. **High-risk operation — revoked attestation**: Execute `RevocationGuard::check_high_risk("principal-B", HighRiskOp::PolicyChange)`. Expect: `Err(RevocationDenial { target_type: Attestation, target_id: "attest-004", enforcement_point: HighRiskOperation })`.
6. **Extension activation — valid**: Execute `RevocationGuard::check_extension_activation("ext-active-001")`. Expect: `Ok(())`.
7. **Extension activation — revoked**: Execute `RevocationGuard::check_extension_activation("ext-003")`. Expect: `Err(RevocationDenial { target_type: Extension, target_id: "ext-003", enforcement_point: ExtensionActivation })`.
8. **Mid-session revocation**: Revoke `tok-valid-001` by appending a new event to the chain. Re-submit `tok-valid-001`. Expect: `Err(RevocationDenial)`.

### Assert
1. Exactly 4 denial audit events emitted (steps 2, 3, 5, 7).
2. Exactly 4 pass audit events emitted (steps 1, 4, 6, and step 8 first use was already counted in step 1).
3. Step 8 produces a denial after the mid-session revocation append.
4. Each audit event contains: `trace_id`, `decision_id`, `enforcement_point`, `target_type`, `target_id`, `outcome`.
5. No `RevocationDenial` error contains plaintext key material — only hashed IDs.
6. The type-system enforcement is validated: attempting to call `token.authorize_action()` on a `SignatureVerifiedToken` (not yet revocation-checked) fails at compile time.

### Teardown
1. Drop the `RevocationChain` and `RevocationGuard`.
2. Verify no dangling references or leaked state.

---

## Structured Logging Fields

### `RevocationCheckEvent` (emitted for every check, pass or fail)
| Field | Type | Example | Required |
|-------|------|---------|----------|
| `timestamp` | `DeterministicTimestamp` | `1708444800000000` | yes |
| `trace_id` | `TraceId` | `"a1b2c3d4..."` | yes |
| `component` | `&'static str` | `"revocation_guard"` | yes |
| `event_type` | `&'static str` | `"revocation_check"` | yes |
| `outcome` | `Outcome` | `"pass"` / `"revoked"` | yes |
| `error_code` | `Option<ErrorCode>` | `"FE-4001"` | if revoked |
| `decision_id` | `DecisionId` | `"dec-rv-001"` | yes |
| `enforcement_point` | `EnforcementPoint` enum | `"token_acceptance"` | yes |
| `target_type` | `RevocationTargetType` | `"token"` / `"key"` | yes |
| `target_id_hash` | `ContentHash` (redacted) | `"blake3:abc..."` | yes |
| `revocation_id` | `Option<EngineObjectId>` | `"eid:rev:xyz..."` | if revoked |
| `transitive` | `bool` | `true` | yes |
| `chain_head_seq` | `u64` | `5` | yes |

---

## Implementation Approach Clarification

### Module Placement
- `src/revocation/guard.rs` — `RevocationGuard` middleware, enforcement point implementations
- `src/revocation/typestate.rs` — `UnverifiedToken`, `SignatureVerifiedToken`, `FullyVerifiedToken` type-state types

### Type-State Token Pipeline
```
UnverifiedToken --[signature_verify]--> SignatureVerifiedToken --[revocation_check]--> FullyVerifiedToken
```
Only `FullyVerifiedToken` implements `AuthorizeAction`. This is enforced at compile time — no runtime bypass possible.

### Transitive Revocation Algorithm
```
fn is_effectively_revoked(target_id) -> bool {
    if chain.is_revoked(target_id) { return true; }
    if let Some(issuer_key) = resolve_issuer_key(target_id) {
        return chain.is_revoked(issuer_key);
    }
    false
}
```
Single-level transitivity (issuer key only). Deeper delegation chains are checked by the delegation verification module (bd-3u7).

### No-Bypass Enforcement
Implement as a mandatory `Layer` / middleware that wraps the 3 enforcement points. The runtime API does not expose raw `accept_token()` — only `guard.check_and_accept_token()`. Module visibility (`pub(crate)`) prevents direct access to internals.

title: [10.11] Emit proof-carrying recovery artifacts for degraded-mode repairs and rejected trust transitions.
description:
## Plan Reference
- **Section**: 10.11 item 32 (FrankenSQLite-Inspired Runtime Systems Track)
- **9G Cross-ref**: 9G.10 — O(Delta) anti-entropy + proof-carrying recovery
- **Top-10 Links**: #5 (Supply-chain trust fabric), #9 (Adversarial security corpus), #10 (Provenance + revocation fabric)

## What
Emit proof-carrying recovery artifacts for degraded-mode repairs and rejected trust transitions. Every recovery action (gap fill, state repair, forced reconciliation, trust restoration) and every rejected trust transition (failed epoch promotion, rejected revocation, failed attestation) produces a machine-verifiable artifact that proves what was repaired, why, and how the repair is consistent with the trust model.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Define a \`RecoveryArtifact\` schema:
   - \`artifact_id\`: content-addressed identifier (Tier 2 ContentHash).
   - \`artifact_type\`: enum of recovery types: \`GapFill\`, \`StateRepair\`, \`ForcedReconciliation\`, \`TrustRestoration\`, \`RejectedEpochPromotion\`, \`RejectedRevocation\`, \`FailedAttestation\`.
   - \`trigger\`: what caused the recovery (reconciliation failure, integrity check failure, operator intervention, automatic fallback).
   - \`before_state\`: snapshot or hash of the state before recovery.
   - \`after_state\`: snapshot or hash of the state after recovery.
   - \`proof_bundle\`: collection of proof elements that verify the recovery is valid:
     - MMR consistency proofs (from bd-2h2) showing the recovered state is consistent with the known-good prefix.
     - Hash-chain verification results for the decision marker stream (bd-3e7).
     - Evidence-entry hashes for the decision that triggered recovery.
     - Epoch validity checks for all artifacts involved in the recovery.
   - \`operator_actions\`: any manual operator actions included in the recovery, with signed authorization.
   - \`trace_id\`, \`epoch_id\`, \`timestamp\`.
2. Verification API: \`verify_recovery(artifact: &RecoveryArtifact) -> Result<RecoveryVerdict, VerificationError>\` that mechanically checks all proof elements and returns a verdict (valid/invalid with reasons).
3. Artifact persistence: recovery artifacts are persisted to durable storage and linked from the decision marker stream (bd-3e7) as markers of type \`Recovery\`.
4. Export: recovery artifacts support export in a standard format for external audit tools and incident response teams.
5. Rejected trust transitions: when a trust transition is rejected (e.g., epoch promotion fails validation, revocation is rejected due to stale attestation), a \`RejectedTransition\` artifact is emitted with: the attempted transition, the rejection reason, the validation checks that failed, and the corrective action taken (degrade to safe mode, alert operator, retry with corrected inputs).
6. All recovery artifacts are signed with the current epoch's authentication key (Tier 3 AuthenticityHash via bd-2ta).

## Rationale
Degraded-mode operations and recovery actions are the highest-risk moments in a distributed trust system. Without proof-carrying artifacts, there is no way to verify after the fact that a recovery was correct, that no state was lost, or that a rejected transition was properly handled. The 9G.10 contract requires that every repair is machine-verifiable so that operational credibility is maintained and incident forensics are comprehensive. This directly supports Section 3.2 item 9 (machine-verifiable repair artifacts) and the evidence-backed operational readiness requirement (Phase E exit gate).

## Testing Requirements
- **Unit tests**: Verify recovery artifact schema completeness. Verify proof bundle generation includes all required elements. Verify \`verify_recovery\` accepts valid artifacts and rejects tampered artifacts.
- **Property tests**: Generate random recovery scenarios, produce artifacts, tamper with random elements, and verify detection.
- **Integration tests**: Trigger a reconciliation failure (via bd-117 fallback), execute recovery, verify the recovery artifact is valid and linked in the marker stream. Trigger a rejected epoch promotion and verify the rejection artifact.
- **Export tests**: Export recovery artifacts and verify they can be parsed and verified by an external tool (verifier CLI from 10.12).
- **Logging/observability**: Recovery events carry: \`artifact_id\`, \`artifact_type\`, \`trigger\`, \`verification_verdict\`, \`trace_id\`, \`epoch_id\`.

## Implementation Notes
- Proof bundles should be assembled lazily: collect proof elements during the recovery process and bundle them at the end.
- Use the MMR proof library (bd-2h2) for consistency proofs and the hash chain verification from bd-3e7.
- Recovery artifacts should be compact enough for network transfer (proofs are O(log n), not O(n)).
- Consider a recovery-artifact viewer in the operator console (via frankentui, 10.14).

## Dependencies
- Depends on: bd-2n6 (anti-entropy reconciliation triggers recovery), bd-117 (fallback protocol produces recovery context), bd-2h2 (MMR proofs for consistency verification), bd-3e7 (marker stream for linking), bd-4hf (hash strategy), bd-2ta (authentication key for signing).
- Blocks: bd-yi6 (phase gates require proof-carrying recovery validation).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Implement the full objective with deterministic behavior, explicit failure semantics, and safe fallback/rollback rules.
- Add focused unit tests for normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid or adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
- Add integration and/or end-to-end test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions, degraded mode, and recovery behavior with deterministic fixtures.
- Emit structured logs with stable keys (trace_id, decision_id, policy_id, component, event, outcome, error_code) and assert critical events in tests.
- Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, evidence pointers, replay pointers, benchmark/check outputs) plus clear operator verification steps.
- Ensure heavy Rust build/test execution paths are documented and run through rch wrappers when implementation begins.

title: [REVIEW] Fleet de-escalation flag is persisted but not wired to live containment recovery
description:
Reality-check scope: fleet containment/quarantine recovery claims versus policy_as_data_security and containment execution paths.

Observed gap:
- policy_as_data_security::SecurityPlaybook includes allows_deescalation and tests verify the field serializes/preserves correctly.
- Fresh scan found no obvious live policy path that performs fleet de-escalation or recovery based on allows_deescalation; current evidence mostly proves data-model preservation and counterfactual replay behavior, not operational de-escalation.
- docs/audit/MODES_OF_REASONING_REPORT_AND_ANALYSIS_OF_PROJECT.md previously flagged this as a medium latent risk: containment may be a permanent ratchet.
- br search found no open de-escalation containment bead.

User impact:
Operators need a safe, auditable path for false-positive recovery. A one-way quarantine/containment ratchet can turn conservative security policy into avoidable outage risk, while an undocumented manual bypass can undermine auditability.

Expected fix:
Design and implement a fail-closed fleet de-escalation path that is explicitly policy-gated, quorum/evidence backed, and replayable. If de-escalation is intentionally out of scope, remove or downgrade claims and document the permanent-ratchet behavior clearly.

5. Add an e2e/replay script with detailed logs for quarantine -> reviewed -> de-escalated and quarantine -> denied paths, including artifact paths and stable failure codes.
6. Update docs/operator runbooks so users know how safe recovery works and what remains intentionally irreversible.

- Unit: policy gate denies de-escalation unless allows_deescalation and all evidence/quorum constraints hold.
- Integration/e2e: deterministic replay of a false-positive quarantine recovery with structured logs and receipt verification.

description:
## Plan Reference

## What
Enforce the one-lever-per-change performance policy in CI and workflow. Each optimization commit changes exactly one variable, with before/after evidence and semantic equivalence proof.

## Detailed Requirements
- CI gate: optimization PRs must include baseline/after benchmark data for the specific optimization
- One lever rule: each optimization commit changes one thing (algorithm, data structure, layout, etc.)

- Isomorphism artifacts: record ordering/tie-break semantics per 9C.1 isomorphism ledger

- Rollback readiness: each optimization must include rollback instructions

## Rationale
Per 9D: 'Implement one lever per commit with opportunity score >= 2.0. Prove isomorphism. Verify against golden outputs and re-profile.' This discipline prevents the common failure mode where multiple simultaneous changes make it impossible to attribute improvements or debug regressions. It turns performance engineering into a measurable scientific practice.

- CI integration test: PR with multiple optimization levers is flagged/rejected

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
ENHANCEMENT (PearlTower audit): Adding implementation specifics for CI gate, ledger schema, and evidence format.

## CI Gate Implementation
The one-lever-per-change policy is enforced by a CI check script (scripts/check_one_lever.sh) that:
1. Parses git diff to identify changed files and classify them into 'lever categories': (a) execution-path changes (parser, IR, interpreter, optimizer), (b) GC/memory changes, (c) security/policy changes, (d) benchmark infrastructure changes, (e) configuration/tuning changes.
2. A commit touching files in more than one lever category is flagged as MULTI_LEVER_VIOLATION.
3. Exemptions: documentation-only changes, test-only changes, and CI infrastructure changes are exempt.
4. Override: A commit message containing '[multi-lever: REASON]' bypasses the gate but is logged in the isomorphism ledger.

## Isomorphism Ledger Schema
```
PerformanceChange {
  change_id: EngineObjectId,
  commit_sha: String,
  lever_category: LeverCategory,  // enum: Execution, Memory, Security, Benchmark, Config
  baseline_benchmark_run_id: EngineObjectId,
  post_change_benchmark_run_id: EngineObjectId,
  delta_summary: BTreeMap<String, f64>,  // metric_name -> percentage_change
  is_multi_lever: bool,
  override_reason: Option<String>,
  timestamp: u64,
}
```

## Evidence Bundle Format
Each performance-relevant commit produces an evidence bundle:
- before.json: benchmark results before the change (from CI baseline cache)
- after.json: benchmark results after the change
- delta.json: computed deltas with statistical significance (p-value, confidence interval)
- lever_classification.json: which files changed and their lever categories
- All files use deterministic JSON serialization (sorted keys) for content-addressable storage.

comments.author: Jeffrey Emanuel
comments.text:
PearlTower architectural scoping (releasing claim — too large for remaining session bandwidth):

## What 'minimal viable' actually requires

The TODO at baseline_interpreter.rs:3840 stubs three independently substantial pieces:

1. **Synchronous body execution + Promise resolution.** Hook into the existing call-frame dispatch (~140 lines starting at line 3873 for non-async functions) to actually invoke the function body. Need a new `CallFrame` discriminator (e.g., `async_promise: Option<u32>` carrying the result_promise id) so that the normal Return path resolves the promise with the return value instead of writing to dst. Throw becomes promise rejection. This is the smallest piece and makes `async function f() { return 42; }` actually work — but only for bodies that never `await`.

2. **Await suspension protocol.** `await x` needs to: (a) save IP/registers/scope into the AsyncFunctionObject, (b) attach a continuation to the awaited Promise (or resolve immediately if x is non-thenable), (c) yield control back to the event loop. The existing `AsyncFunctionPhase::SuspendedAwait` variant exists but no opcode wires it up.

3. **Resume-from-await on microtask drain.** A microtask queue drains when JS dispatch reaches a yield point. On drain, find AsyncFunctionObjects with phase=SuspendedAwait whose awaited promise is now settled, restore their IP/registers/scope, push back into the dispatch loop. Promise resolution callbacks need to enqueue microtasks rather than synchronously invoking handlers.

## Suggested decomposition

Split into three children:
- bd-2lg6f.1 — sync-async body execution (piece 1, test: async fn returning 42 resolves promise to 42)
- bd-2lg6f.2 — await opcode + suspension state save (piece 2)
- bd-2lg6f.3 — microtask drain + resume (piece 3, cross-cuts promise_model)

Each is doable in a single session with focused tests. .1 should land first since .2 and .3 share its call-frame changes.

## Existing scaffolding

- AsyncFunctionObject (line 656) — has saved_ip/saved_registers/saved_register_base/phase/result_promise. Designed for this.
- AsyncFunctionPhase enum (line 625) — SuspendedStart/SuspendedAwait/Executing/Completed.
- promise_store (line 1832) — exists, create() returns Promise(handle).
- Generator code path (line 3798) — analogous structure; check whether await can reuse suspend/resume scaffolding.

## Why I'm releasing

This session has shipped 6 P1 closes. The async runtime piece is roughly equal in scope to all six combined. A fresh agent with full context budget will do better work on this than I will at session tail.

title: [10.15] Implement static upper-bound authority analyzer from capability-typed IR + manifest intents.
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.15 (Delta Moonshots Execution Track), subsection 9I.5 (PLAS), item 2 of 14.

## What
Implement the static upper-bound authority analyzer that computes a conservative capability upper bound from capability-typed IR and declared manifest intents.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Analysis pipeline:
   - Input: capability-typed IR (IR2 CapabilityIR) effect graph + extension manifest declared intents.
   - Compute reachable capability set using lattice reachability analysis over the effect graph.
   - Identify capability-typed hostcall sites and their statically determinable capability requirements.
   - Produce conservative upper bound: set of capabilities that could possibly be exercised on any execution path.
2. Analysis precision:
   - Must be sound (no false negatives -- every actually needed capability is in the upper bound).
   - Should minimize false positives (capabilities in the upper bound that are never actually needed) through path-sensitive analysis where tractable.
   - Report precision metrics: estimated over-approximation ratio vs. manifest-declared capabilities.
3. Output artifact:
   - Structured analysis report: `extension_id`, `upper_bound_capability_set`, `per_capability_evidence` (which IR nodes/paths require this capability), `analysis_method`, `precision_estimate`, `analysis_duration`.
   - Report feeds directly into the PLAS synthesis pipeline as the static evidence input.
4. Performance constraints: analysis must complete within configurable time budget (fail-open to manifest-declared set if budget exceeded, with warning).
5. Incremental analysis: support re-analysis on IR changes with minimal recomputation.

## Rationale
From 9I.5: "Static pass computes a conservative authority upper bound using capability lattice reachability and effect-flow analysis." The static analyzer is the first pass in the PLAS pipeline, providing the formal foundation from which dynamic ablation can further tighten the capability envelope. Without a sound static upper bound, the ablation engine lacks a safe starting point.

## Testing Requirements
- Unit tests: analysis on minimal IR graphs with known capability requirements, verify soundness (no needed capability missing), verify precision on simple cases.
- Integration tests: analyze representative extension IRs and verify upper bounds are correct against known capability usage.
- Adversarial tests: extensions with obfuscated capability usage patterns, dynamic dispatch that complicates static analysis.
- Benchmark: analysis time on representative extension sizes must stay within CI budget.

## Implementation Notes
- Build on the capability-typed IR infrastructure from 10.2 (IR2 CapabilityIR).
- Consider using abstract interpretation or dataflow analysis frameworks.
- Path sensitivity can be enabled/disabled per analysis budget for precision/performance tradeoff.

## Dependencies
- 10.2 (IR2 CapabilityIR with capability typing and effect metadata).
- 10.5 (capability lattice definitions).
- bd-2w9w (PLAS artifact schema for output format).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Implement the full objective with deterministic behavior, explicit failure semantics, and safe fallback/rollback rules.
- Add focused unit tests for normal paths, boundary conditions, invalid or adversarial inputs, and invariant enforcement.
- Add integration and/or end-to-end test scripts that exercise lifecycle transitions, degraded mode, and recovery behavior with deterministic fixtures.
- Emit structured logs with stable keys (trace_id, decision_id, policy_id, component, event, outcome, error_code) and assert critical events in tests.
- Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, evidence pointers, replay pointers, benchmark/check outputs) plus clear operator verification steps.
- Ensure heavy Rust build/test execution paths are documented and run through rch wrappers when implementation begins.

title: [10.15] Define privacy-learning contract for fleet calibration (`feature schema`, update policy, clipping strategy, DP budget semantics, secure-aggregation requirements).
description:
## Plan Reference
Section 10.15 (Delta Moonshots Execution Track), subsection 9I.2 (Privacy-Preserving Fleet Learning Layer), item 1 of 4.

## What
Define the privacy-learning contract that governs how fleet-wide calibration data is collected, aggregated, and consumed without centralizing raw tenant-sensitive traces.

## Detailed Requirements
1. Contract schema must specify:
   - `feature_schema`: typed definition of local model update/summary statistic fields (calibration residuals, drift indicators, action outcomes, false-positive/false-negative signals) with versioning and backward-compatibility rules.
   - `update_policy`: rules governing when local updates are computed, how frequently they are submitted, and minimum sample requirements before submission.
   - `clipping_strategy`: per-feature clipping bounds (L2 norm, per-coordinate, adaptive) to bound sensitivity before noise addition.
   - `dp_budget_semantics`: explicit `epsilon`, `delta` parameters per epoch, composition accounting method (basic, advanced, Renyi, zCDP), total lifetime budget, and hard fail-closed behavior on exhaustion.
   - `secure_aggregation_requirements`: minimum participant threshold for aggregation, dropout tolerance, cryptographic protocol requirements (e.g., secret sharing scheme, threshold), and coordinator trust model.
2. Contract must be machine-readable (canonical JSON schema) and human-auditable.
3. Versioned with epoch identifiers; contract changes require signed governance approval and propagation to all fleet participants.
4. Include explicit data-retention and deletion semantics for intermediate aggregation state.
5. Define clear separation between learning state (stochastic) and decision state (deterministic): live decision paths consume only signed snapshot artifacts.

## Rationale
From 9I.2: "Centralized telemetry learning often fails adoption due to confidentiality and compliance constraints. A privacy-preserving approach enables large-scale collective intelligence while keeping privacy risk explicitly measured, budgeted, and enforceable." The contract is the foundational specification that makes all privacy guarantees auditable and enforceable.

## Testing Requirements
- Unit tests: parse valid/invalid contracts, enforce budget constraint validation, reject contracts with impossible composition parameters, validate feature schema backward compatibility.
- Integration tests: contract propagation to simulated fleet participants, verify all participants enforce identical clipping and budget rules.
- Property tests: verify that any contract satisfying the schema also satisfies the stated DP guarantees under the declared composition method.

## Implementation Notes
- Use the reproducibility contract pattern from 10.1 for contract versioning and evidence linkage.
- Feature schema should align with the evidence/telemetry schemas from 10.5 and 10.11.
- Consider using Renyi DP or zCDP for tighter composition, but document the composition method explicitly in the contract.

## Dependencies
- 10.5 (evidence stream schemas for telemetry/calibration data).
- 10.10 (deterministic serialization for contract encoding).
- 10.1 (governance contract patterns).

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Implement the full objective with explicit deterministic behavior, failure semantics, and rollback constraints where applicable.

5. Produce reproducibility artifacts (run manifest, replay/evidence pointers, benchmark/check outputs) and document operator verification steps.

title: Align baseline String.prototype.charAt with UTF-16 indexing
description: Review of commit 4da3104a found String.prototype.charAt in the baseline interpreter is still indexed with Rust chars instead of JavaScript UTF-16 code units. The active arm at crates/franken-engine/src/baseline_interpreter.rs:7764 collects s.chars(), so non-BMP strings like emoji are treated as one scalar instead of two UTF-16 code units, while stdlib.rs:2409 already uses utf16_code_unit_at/utf16_materialize. The active arm also returns an empty string when no index argument is present, but charAt() should default to index 0. The duplicate later arm at :17294 handles the default but is unreachable and also uses chars(). Fix the active baseline arm to share the stdlib UTF-16 behavior and add tests for omitted index, BMP, non-BMP/surrogate behavior, negative index, and out of bounds.
close_reason: done: Aligned charAt with UTF-16 indexing semantics. Fixed surrogate pair handling to use UTF-16 code units instead of Unicode code points. Consolidated duplicate implementations. Added comprehensive test coverage. Commit: 3b448a39
